title: Chapter 3: Integration and the Fundamental Theorem
text:
Integration is the reverse process of differentiation, but it also solves the problem of finding the area under a curve.


We want to find the area under the curve \(y = f(x)\) from \(x = a\) to \(x = b\). We divide the interval \([a, b]\) into \(n\) subintervals of width \(\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}\) and choose sample points \(x_i^*\) in each subinterval.
The area is approximated by a Riemann Sum: \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i^*) \Delta x \]
The definite integral of \(f\) from \(a\) to \(b\) is the limit of this sum as \(n \to \infty\):
\[ \int_a^b f(x) \, dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i^*) \Delta x \]



The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC) establishes the connection between the two branches of calculus: differential and integral.
Part 1: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\), then the function \(g\) defined by: \[ g(x) = \int_a^x f(t) \, dt \quad \text{for } a \le x \le b \] is continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\), and \(g'(x) = f(x)\). This means the derivative of an integral of a function is the function itself.
Part 2: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\), then: \[ \int_a^b f(x) \, dx = F(b) - F(a) \] where \(F\) is any antiderivative of \(f\) (that is, \(F' = f\)).



Finding antiderivatives can be much harder than finding derivatives. We use several techniques:

Substitution Rule (Reverse Chain Rule): If \(u = g(x)\), then \(\int f(g(x))g'(x) \, dx = \int f(u) \, du\).
Integration by Parts (Reverse Product Rule): \(\int u \, dv = uv - \int v \, du\).
Trigonometric Substitution: Used for integrals involving \(\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\), \(\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}\), etc.
Partial Fractions: Used to integrate rational functions by breaking them into simpler fractions.

title: Chapter 2: Derivatives and Rates of Change
text:
While limits describe where a function is heading, derivatives describe how fast it is changing at any given instant.


The derivative of a function \(f\) at a number \(a\), denoted by \(f'(a)\), is:
\[ f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h} \]
If this limit exists, we say \(f\) is differentiable at \(a\). Geometrically, \(f'(a)\) represents the slope of the tangent line to the curve \(y = f(x)\) at the point \((a, f(a))\).
Physically, if \(f(t)\) represents the position of a particle at time \(t\), then \(f'(t)\) represents the instantaneous velocity of the particle.



Calculating limits using the definition is tedious. We use proven rules to find derivatives efficiently:

Power Rule: If \(f(x) = x^n\) where \(n\) is any real number, then \(f'(x) = n x^{n-1}\).
Exponential Function: \(\frac{d}{dx} e^x = e^x\).
Product Rule: \(\frac{d}{dx} [f(x)g(x)] = f(x)g'(x) + g(x)f'(x)\)
Quotient Rule: \(\frac{d}{dx} \left[ \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \right] = \frac{g(x)f'(x) - f(x)g'(x)}{[g(x)]^2}\)
Chain Rule: If \(y = f(u)\) and \(u = g(x)\), then \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}\). Alternatively, \(\frac{d}{dx} [f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))g'(x)\).




Sometimes a relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) is expressed implicitly, like \(x^2 + y^2 = 25\). We can find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) without solving for \(y\) by differentiating both sides with respect to \(x\) and applying the Chain Rule to terms involving \(y\).



One of the most important theoretical results in differential calculus:
Theorem: If \(f\) is a continuous function on the closed interval \([a, b]\) and differentiable on the open interval \((a, b)\), then there exists a number \(c\) in \((a, b)\) such that:
\[ f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a} \]
This states that at some point \(c\), the instantaneous rate of change (the tangent slope) is exactly equal to the average rate of change (the secant slope) over the interval.

text: I am a senior HBSc student at the University of Toronto (UTSC), pursuing a Physics and Mathematics Specialist with a Minor in Statistics (former Biochemistry Major). My academic journey is driven by how mathematical structures underpin the physical world and how computational tools model complex systems.

title: About Me
text:
Background

Mathematical Analysis: Real & Complex Analysis, Functional Analysis, Topology, Axiomatic Set Theory
Modeling: ODE/PDE, Stochastic Processes, Convex & Linear Optimization, Numerical Methods
Scientific Computing: Python (NumPy, SciPy, Pandas), R, MATLAB
Physics: Quantum Mechanics, Electrodynamics, Classical Mechanics, Thermal Physics
Life Sciences: Biochemistry, Genetics, Molecular Biology, Organic Chemistry

Beyond the classroom I am a software enthusiast. I build full-stack web applications, automated pipelines, developer tools, and interactive visualizations. I enjoy translating complex scientific concepts into interactive code.

title: Chekhov Reading Guide: ‘Без заглавия’ (Without a Title)
text:
Anton Chekhov’s “Без заглавия” (Without a Title), published in 1888, is a subtle, humorous fable about human nature, temptation, and the paradoxical allure of worldly vices.
Set in a 5th-century desert monastery, the story follows a group of holy monks led by an elderly abbot who plays the organ, writes poetry, and preaches with divine eloquence. When a drunken traveler tells them of the moral degradation and sinful pleasures of the nearby city, the abbot feels called to go and preach repentance. Upon his return months later, he describes the city’s corruption—but does so with such vivid, artistic, and passionate descriptions of its beauty, wine, and semi-naked women that by the next morning, all the monks have run away to the city.

В V веке, как и теперь, каждое утро вставало солнце и каждый вечер оно ложилось спать. Утром, когда с росою целовались первые лучи, земля оживала, воздух наполнялся звуками радости, восторга и надежды, а вечером та же земля затихала и тонула в суровых потемках. День походил на день, ночь на ночь. Изредка набегала туча и сердито гремел гром, или падала с неба зазевавшаяся звезда, или пробегал бледный монах и рассказывал братии, что недалеко от монастыря он видел тигра — и только, а потом опять день походил на день, ночь на ночь.
Монахи работали и молились богу, а их настоятель-старик играл на органе, сочинял латинские стихи и писал ноты. Этот чудный старик обладал необычайным даром. Он играл на органе с таким искусством, что даже самые старые монахи, у которых к концу жизни притупился слух, не могли удержать слез, когда из его кельи доносились звуки органа. Когда он говорил о чем-нибудь, даже самом обыкновенном, например, о деревьях, зверях или о море, его нельзя было слушать без улыбки или без слез, и казалось, что в душе его звучали такие же струны, как и в органе. Если же он гневался, или предавался сильной радости, или начинал говорить о чем-нибудь ужасном и великом, то страстное вдохновение овладевало им, на сверкающих глазах выступали слезы, лицо румянилось, голос гремел, как гром, и монахи, слушая его, чувствовали, как его вдохновение сковывало их души; в такие великолепные, чудные минуты власть его бывала безгранична, и если бы он приказал своим старцам броситься в море, то они все до одного с восторгом поспешили бы исполнить его волю.
Каково же поэтому было удивление монахов, когда однажды ночью в их ворота постучался человек, который оказался горожанином и самым обыкновенным грешником, любящим жизнь. Прежде чем попросить у настоятеля благословения и помолиться, этот человек потребовал вина и есть. На вопрос, как он попал из города в пустыню, он отвечал длинной охотничьей историей: пошел на охоту, выпил лишнее и заблудился. На предложение поступить в монахи и спасти свою душу он ответил улыбкой и словами: «Я вам не товарищ».
Наевшись и напившись, он оглядел монахов, которые прислуживали ему, покачал укоризненно головой и сказал:
— Ничего вы не делаете, монахи. Только и знаете, что едите да пьете. Разве так спасают душу? Подумайте: в то время, как вы сидите тут в покое, едите, пьете и мечтаете о блаженстве, ваши ближние погибают и идут в ад. Поглядите-ка, что делается в городе! Одни умирают с голоду, другие, не зная, куда девать свое золото, топят себя в разврате и гибнут, как мухи, вязнущие в меду. Нет в людях ни веры, ни правды! Чье же дело спасать их? Чье дело проповедовать? Не мне ли, который от утра до вечера пьян? Разве смиренный дух, любящее сердце и веру бог дал вам на то, чтобы вы сидели здесь в четырех стенах и ничего не делали?



Смиренный (Smirenny): Humble / submissive.

Пьяные слова горожанина были дерзки и неприличны, но странным образом подействовали на настоятеля. Старик переглянулся со своими монахами, побледнел и сказал:
— Братья, а ведь он правду говорит! В самом деле, бедные люди по неразумию и слабости гибнут в пороке и неверии, а мы не двигаемся с места, как будто нас это не касается. Отчего бы мне не пойти и не напомнить им о Христе, которого они забыли?
Слова горожанина увлекли старика; на другой же день он взял свою трость, простился с братией и отправился в город. И монахи остались без музыки, без его речей и стихов.
Проскучали они месяц, другой, а старик не возвращался. Наконец после третьего месяца послышался знакомый стук его трости. Монахи бросились к нему навстречу и осыпали его вопросами, но он, вместо того чтобы обрадоваться им, горько заплакал и не сказал ни одного слова. Монахи заметили: он сильно состарился и похудел; лицо его было утомлено и выражало глубокую скорбь, а когда он заплакал, то имел вид человека, которого оскорбили.
Монахи тоже заплакали и с участием стали расспрашивать, зачем он плачет, отчего лицо его так угрюмо, но он не сказал ни слова и заперся в своей келье. Семь дней сидел он у себя, ничего не ел, не пил, не играл на органе и плакал. На стук в его дверь и на просьбы монахов выйти и поделиться с ними своею печалью он отвечал глубоким молчанием.
Наконец он вышел. Собрав вокруг себя всех монахов, он с заплаканным лицом и с выражением скорби и негодования начал рассказывать о том, что было с ним в последние три месяца. Голос его был спокоен, и глаза улыбались, когда он описывал свой путь от монастыря до города. На пути, говорил он, ему пели птицы, журчали ручьи, и сладкие, молодые надежды волновали его душу; он шел и чувствовал себя солдатом, который идет на бой и уверен в победе; мечтая, он шел и слагал стихи и гимны и не заметил, как кончился путь.
Но голос его дрогнул, глаза засверкали, и весь он распалился гневом, когда стал говорить о городе и людях. Никогда в жизни он не видел, даже не дерзал воображать себе то, что он встретил, войдя в город. Только тут, первый раз в жизни, на старости лет, он увидел и понял, как могуч дьявол, как прекрасно зло и как слабы, малодушны и ничтожны люди.



Распалился (Raspalilsya): Flamed up / became hot with passion or anger.

По несчастной случайности, первое жилище, в которое он вошел, был дом разврата. С полсотни человек, имеющих много денег, ели и без меры пили вино. Опьяненные вином, они пели песни и смело говорили страшные, отвратительные слова, которых не решится сказать человек, боящийся бога; безгранично свободные, бодрые, счастливые, они не боялись ни бога, ни дьявола, ни смерти, а говорили и делали всё, что хотели, и шли туда, куда гнала их похоть. А вино, чистое, как янтарь, подернутое золотыми искрами, вероятно, было нестерпимо сладко и пахуче, потому что каждый пивший блаженно улыбался и хотел еще пить. На улыбку человека оно отвечало тоже улыбкой и, когда его пили, радостно искрилось, точно знало, какую дьявольскую прелесть таит оно в своей сладости.
Старик, всё больше распаляясь и плача от гнева, продолжал описывать то, что он видел. На столе, среди пировавших, говорил он, стояла полунагая блудница. Трудно представить себе и найти в природе что-нибудь более прекрасное и пленительное. Эта гадина, молодая, длинноволосая, смуглая, с черными глазами и с жирными губами, бесстыдная и наглая, оскалила свои белые, как снег, зубы и улыбалась, как будто хотела сказать: «Поглядите, какая я наглая, какая красивая!» Шелк и парча красивыми складками спускались с ее плеч, но красота не хотела прятаться под одеждой, а, как молодая зелень из весенней почвы, жадно пробивалась сквозь складки. Наглая женщина пила вино, пела песни и отдавалась всякому, кто только хотел.
Далее старик, гневно потрясая руками, описал конские ристалища, бой быков, театры, мастерские художников, где пишут и лепят из глины нагих женщин. Говорил он вдохновенно, красиво и звучно, точно играл на невидимых струнах, а монахи, оцепеневшие, жадно внимали его речам и задыхались от восторга… Описав все прелести дьявола, красоту зла и пленительную грацию отвратительного женского тела, старик проклял дьявола, повернул назад и скрылся за своею дверью…
Когда он на другое утро вышел из кельи, в монастыре не оставалось ни одного монаха. Все они бежали в город.

title: The Poet of Transformation: The Life, Works, and Exile of Ovid
text:
Publius Ovidius Naso (20 March 43 BC – 17/18 AD), known to the English-speaking world as Ovid, was one of the most prolific, versatile, and influential poets of the Roman Golden Age. Alongside Virgil and Horace, he forms the canonical triumvirate of Latin literature.
Unlike Virgil, who wrote the solemn, state-sanctioned epic of Rome’s founding (The Aeneid), Ovid was a poet of wit, sensuality, psychology, and transformation. He was a master of the elegiac couplet, bringing a playful, irreverent, and deeply human voice to Roman society.
His life was divided into two distinct halves: a stellar career in Rome as the city’s favorite literary celebrity, followed by a sudden, devastating exile to the remote edge of the Roman Empire on the Black Sea.

title: The Poet of Transformation: The Life, Works, and Exile of Ovid
text:
Publius Ovidius Naso (20 March 43 BC – 17/18 AD), known to the English-speaking world as Ovid, was one of the most prolific, versatile, and influential poets of the Roman Golden Age. Alongside Virgil and Horace, he forms the canonical triumvirate of Latin literature.
Unlike Virgil, who wrote the solemn, state-sanctioned epic of Rome’s founding (The Aeneid), Ovid was a poet of wit, sensuality, psychology, and transformation. He was a master of the elegiac couplet, bringing a playful, irreverent, and deeply human voice to Roman society.
His life was divided into two distinct halves: a stellar career in Rome as the city’s favorite literary celebrity, followed by a sudden, devastating exile to the remote edge of the Roman Empire on the Black Sea.

title: The Poet of Transformation: The Life, Works, and Exile of Ovid
text:
1. Major Works
Ovid’s literary output was vast and diverse, spanning love poetry, mythological epics, and elegies of despair.

A. Metamorphoses (The Transformations)
Ovid’s magnum opus is the “Metamorphoses”, a fifteen-book mythological epic written in dactylic hexameter (the meter of traditional epic poetry).

The Core Concept: Unlike traditional epics that follow a single hero (like Achilles or Aeneas), the Metamorphoses is a collective narrative of over 250 myths, linked by the theme of physical transformation (metamorphosis).
The Chronology: The poem traces the history of the cosmos from its creation out of Chaos to the deification of Julius Caesar, weaving Greek and Roman myths into a continuous, flowing song (carmen perpetuum).
Key Myths Explored:

Apollo and Daphne: The god of music is humbled by Cupid and falls in love with a nymph who escapes him by transforming into a laurel tree.
Daedalus and Icarus: The master craftsman builds wings of wax and feathers to escape Crete, but his son flies too close to the sun.
Narcissus and Echo: A beautiful youth falls in love with his own reflection and wastes away, while the nymph Echo fades until only her voice remains.
Pygmalion: A sculptor carves a statue of his ideal woman out of ivory and falls in love with it; Venus brings the statue to life.




B. Love Poetry (Amores and Ars Amatoria)
Before writing his epic, Ovid established himself as Rome’s premiere poet of romance. * Amores (The Loves): A collection of elegiac poems detailing his dramatic, humorous, and volatile love affair with a fictional mistress named Corinna. * Ars Amatoria (The Art of Love): A three-book didactic poem (a mock instruction manual) on how to find, seduce, and keep a lover in Rome. Books 1 and 2 are addressed to men, while Book 3 is addressed to women. This work was highly controversial, as it directly subverted the conservative moral reforms of Emperor Augustus.


C. Heroides (The Heroines)
A highly innovative work consisting of fictional letters written by famous mythological women to the husbands or lovers who abandoned them. Examples include Penelope writing to Ulysses, Dido to Aeneas, and Ariadne to Theseus. The Heroides showcases Ovid’s deep psychological empathy, giving voice and interior depth to figures usually sidelined in male-centric epics.


D. Fasti (The Calendar)
A poetic treatment of the Roman calendar, explaining the origins of Roman festivals, astronomical patterns, and religious rites. Ovid completed only six books (January through June) before his exile interrupted his work.


E. Exile Poetry (Tristia and Epistulae ex Ponto)
Written after his banishment, these collections of letters and poems detail his grief, his struggle to survive in a hostile environment, and his desperate pleas for pardon. * Tristia (Sorrows): Five books of elegies describing his journey to exile, his loneliness, and his defense of his poetry. * Epistulae ex Ponto (Letters from the Black Sea): Four books of letters addressed to specific friends in Rome, pleading for their help in securing his return or a transfer to a less harsh location.

title: The Poet of Transformation: The Life, Works, and Exile of Ovid
section: 2. The Mystery of Exile: Carmen et Error
text:
2. The Mystery of Exile: Carmen et Error
In 8 AD, at the height of his fame, Ovid was suddenly banished by Emperor Augustus to Tomis (modern-day Constanța, Romania), a remote outpost on the edge of the Roman world inhabited by local tribes.
Unlike a citizen who suffered exsilium (which involved loss of property and citizenship), Ovid was subjected to relegatio, meaning he kept his property and rights but was forced to remain in his designated place of banishment.
Ovid famously stated that his banishment was due to “carmen et error” (a poem and a mistake):

“Cur aliquid vidi? Cur noxia lumina feci? Cur imprudenti cognita culpa mihi est?” (Why did I see something? Why did I make my eyes guilty? Why was a fault made known to my imprudence?) — Tristia 2.103-104


The Two Pillars of Banishment

The Poem (Carmen): This is universally believed to be the “Ars Amatoria”. Augustus, who was attempting to enforce strict family values and adultery laws through his Leges Juliae, viewed Ovid’s seduction manual as an active encouragement of moral degradation. The book was banned from public libraries.
The Mistake (Error): The nature of Ovid’s error remains one of the greatest mysteries of classical history. Because Ovid refused to specify it to protect his friends and family, historians have posited several theories:

The Imperial Scandal Theory: Ovid may have witnessed or assisted in the adulterous affairs of Augustus’s granddaughter, Julia the Younger, who was banished in the exact same year (8 AD) for adultery.
The Conspiracy Theory: Ovid may have accidentally overheard or stumbled upon a political conspiracy involving Livia (Augustus’s wife) or Tiberius (Augustus’s stepson and successor).
The Cult Theory: Ovid may have witnessed secret, forbidden religious rites.


Ovid spent the last decade of his life in Tomis, freezing in the cold winters and terrified of nomadic raids. Despite his continuous literary appeals, Augustus never pardoned him, and Tiberius ignored his pleas after Augustus’s death. Ovid died in Tomis around 17 or 18 AD.

title: The Poet of Transformation: The Life, Works, and Exile of Ovid
text:
3. Style, Language, and Literary Techniques
Ovid’s style is characterized by a set of distinct features that set him apart from his contemporaries:

Symmetry and Balance: Ovid was a rhetorician. He structured his couplets with meticulous symmetry, often utilizing chiasmus (A-B-B-A word order) and antithesis to create balanced, punchy lines.
Playfulness and Irony: Even when discussing tragic myths, Ovid maintains a light, ironic distance. He frequently pokes fun at the gods, depicting them as driven by petty human lusts, jealousy, and vanity.
Vivid Pictorial Style: Ovid wrote with a visual intensity. His descriptions of physical transformations (e.g., Daphne’s arms turning into branches, Narcissus dissolving into a flower) are written with cinematic detail, capturing the exact transition states.
Psychological Realism: Ovid excelled at writing internal soliloquies. His characters debate with themselves, weigh moral choices, and struggle with conflicting passions (e.g., Medea’s struggle between duty to her father and love for Jason).

title: The Poet of Transformation: The Life, Works, and Exile of Ovid
text:
4. Ovid’s Enduring Legacy
Ovid’s influence on Western art, literature, and culture is immeasurable. During the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, he was the primary source through which Europe learned classical mythology.

Dante Alighieri: Dante places Ovid in Limbo alongside Homer, Horace, and Virgil in The Divine Comedy, and borrows heavily from the Metamorphoses to describe the physical mutations of the thieves in the Inferno.
Geoffrey Chaucer: Chaucer’s The Legend of Good Women and The Canterbury Tales adapt numerous tales from Ovid, and he refers to Ovid simply as “the Clerk of the stories.”
William Shakespeare: Shakespeare was deeply saturated in Ovid. The play-within-a-play in A Midsummer Night’s Dream (Pyramus and Thisbe) is a direct adaptation from Book 4 of the Metamorphoses. Prospero’s famous renunciation speech in The Tempest (“Ye elves of hills, brooks, standing lakes, and groves…”) is a poetic paraphrase of Medea’s incantation in Book 7 of the Metamorphoses.
Visual Arts: Painters like Titian, Bernini, Rubens, and Velázquez drew direct inspiration from Ovid’s narrative descriptions to paint iconic works like Apollo and Daphne, Diana and Actaeon, and The Rape of Europa.

title: Editing Files Fast with Sed: Flags, Regex, and In-Place Modifications
text:
On Linux systems, configuration files are plain text. While you can open a text editor to make modifications, doing so programmatically or quickly from the command line is often more efficient.
sed (Stream Editor) is a utility used to perform basic text transformations on an input stream or file. In this guide, we will analyze essential sed flags, commands, and regular expressions using practical scenarios for editing system configs.

title: Editing Files Fast with Sed: Flags, Regex, and In-Place Modifications
text:
1. Key Sed Flags
Two flags are essential for system configuration tasks:

-i (In-Place): By default, sed prints its output to the terminal screen (stdout) and leaves the original file untouched. The -i flag writes the changes directly back to the file.
-n (Silent/No-Print): By default, sed prints every line of the file after processing. The -n flag suppresses this automatic printing, allowing you to selectively print specific lines (usually combined with the p command).
-E or -r (Extended Regular Expressions): Enables modern, extended regular expressions (ERE) rather than basic regular expressions (BRE). This removes the need to escape parentheses (), braces {}, and plus signs +.
-e (Multiple Scripts): Allows you to chain multiple editing commands sequentially in a single pass.

title: Editing Files Fast with Sed: Flags, Regex, and In-Place Modifications
text:
2. In-Place Editing and Automatic Backups
Modifying files in-place (-i) is extremely convenient, but it carries the risk of corrupting critical configuration files if your regular expression is incorrect. sed provides a built-in mechanism to create a backup file immediately before writing changes.

The GNU vs. BSD/macOS Sed Difference
The syntax for backups differs depending on whether you are on a GNU-based system (like Linux) or a BSD-based system (like macOS):

GNU Sed (Linux)
Under Linux, you can attach the backup suffix directly to the -i flag (with no space):
# Modifies config.conf and creates config.conf.bak as a backup of the original
sed -i.bak 's/port = 80/port = 8080/g' config.conf
To run GNU sed in-place without a backup, use -i by itself:
sed -i 's/old/new/g' file.txt


BSD/macOS Sed
macOS uses the BSD version of sed, which requires an argument for the -i flag specifying the backup extension. Leaving it empty requires an explicit empty string '':
# macOS/BSD: Backup file created with .bak suffix
sed -i '.bak' 's/port = 80/port = 8080/g' config.conf

# macOS/BSD: In-place edit WITHOUT creating a backup
sed -i '' 's/old/new/g' file.txt

title: Editing Files Fast with Sed: Flags, Regex, and In-Place Modifications
text:
3. Real-World Config Examples

Example A: Previewing Specific Lines
Before modifying a file, it is safe practice to inspect its contents.
sed -n '110,114p' ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/keybinds.conf

Syntax Breakdown:

-n: Tells sed not to print the file contents by default.
'110,114p': The range 110,114 targets lines 110 through 114 inclusive. The command p stands for print.
Result: Only lines 110 to 114 of the file are printed to the terminal, serving as a preview.





Example B: Commenting Out Deprecated Options (e.g., ignore_window)
If you need to disable a setting in a config file, you can comment it out by prepending a hash (#) character.
sed -i.bak 's/^\s*ignore_window\s*=.*/# &/' ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/general.conf

Syntax Breakdown:

-i.bak: Edit in-place and create a backup named general.conf.bak.
s/pattern/replacement/: The substitution command.
The Pattern (^\s*ignore_window\s*=.*/):

^ asserts the start of the line.
\s* matches zero or more whitespace characters.
ignore_window matches the exact word.
\s*=\s* matches the equals sign with any surrounding spaces.
.* matches the rest of the line (any parameters after the equals sign).

The Replacement (# &):

The & character represents the entire matched string.
Prepending # comments out the line while keeping its original content intact.






Example C: Deleting Lines, Empty Lines, or Comments
If you want to strip out all comments or empty lines from a configuration file for cleaner viewing:
# Delete all lines starting with #
sed '/^#/d' config.conf

# Delete all empty lines (or lines containing only whitespace)
sed '/^\s*$/d' config.conf

d (Delete): Deletes the matched lines from the stream.




Example D: Chaining Multiple Replacements
If you need to change several settings simultaneously, use the -e flag to specify multiple scripts:
sed -i.bak -e 's/timeout = 300/timeout = 600/' \
           -e 's/debug = true/debug = false/' config.conf



Example E: Appending/Inserting Lines
You can insert new lines of text before or after a specific pattern match:
# Append a line AFTER the matching line (using 'a' for append)
sed '/ssl_enable = true/a \    ssl_port = 443' server.conf

# Insert a line BEFORE the matching line (using 'i' for insert)
sed '/server_name localhost/i \    # Default Server Block' server.conf

title: Editing Files Fast with Sed: Flags, Regex, and In-Place Modifications
section: 4. Substitution Flags: Global, Case-Insensitive, and Specific Lines
text:
4. Substitution Flags: Global, Case-Insensitive, and Specific Lines
The substitution command s/pattern/replacement/flags accepts flags at the end to alter its behavior:








Flag
Meaning
Example




g
Global: Replace all occurrences of the pattern on each line, rather than just the first occurrence.
sed 's/old/new/g'


I
Case-Insensitive: Match the pattern regardless of case.
sed 's/error/WARNING/I'


Line Number
Specific line match: Perform the substitution only on a specific line.
sed '3s/inactive/active/'

title: Editing Files Fast with Sed: Flags, Regex, and In-Place Modifications
text:
5. Summary Checklist for Stream Editing

Dry Run First: Always run your command without -i first to see the stdout preview.
Double Quote for Variables: Use single quotes '' for literal patterns. If you need to expand bash variables, use double quotes "":
PORT=8080
sed -i "s/PORT_PLACEHOLDER/$PORT/g" config.json
Use Alternative Delimiters: If your pattern contains slashes (e.g., URLs or file paths), you can use any character (like |, _, or :) as a delimiter to avoid escaping:
sed 's|/usr/bin|/usr/local/bin|g' paths.txt

title: The Ultimate Guide to Tmux: Terminal Multiplexing Made Easy
text:
If you spend a lot of time in the terminal, you have likely run into the limit of managing multiple terminals, tabs, and windows. This problem is amplified when connecting to remote servers via SSH; if your network connection drops, your running processes die.
Tmux (Terminal Multiplexer) solves these problems. It allows you to run multiple terminal sessions inside a single window, split your screen into panes, and detach sessions so they run in the background even if you log out.

title: The Ultimate Guide to Tmux: Terminal Multiplexing Made Easy
text:
1. Core Concepts of Tmux
Tmux organizes your workflow into three hierarchical structures: 1. Sessions: A session contains one or more windows. A session runs in the background and stays alive until the server restarts or you explicitly kill it. 2. Windows: Similar to tabs in a web browser, a window occupies the entire display screen. 3. Panes: You can split any window into multiple rectangular areas called panes, each running its own shell.

title: The Ultimate Guide to Tmux: Terminal Multiplexing Made Easy
section: 2. Managing Sessions from the Command Line
text:
2. Managing Sessions from the Command Line
Before launching tmux, you manage sessions using the standard system terminal.
# Start a new session with a random name
tmux

# Start a new session with a descriptive name (Recommended)
tmux new -s dev

# List all active tmux sessions
tmux ls

# Attach to the last active session
tmux a

# Attach to a specific named session
tmux attach -t dev

# Kill/Delete a specific session
tmux kill-session -t dev

# Kill all active tmux sessions
tmux kill-server

title: The Ultimate Guide to Tmux: Terminal Multiplexing Made Easy
text:
3. Session Navigation: The Prefix Key
Once inside a Tmux session, all keyboard commands must be preceded by the Prefix key. By default, the prefix key is:
\[\text{Prefix} = \text{Ctrl} + \text{b}\]
To execute a command, press Ctrl + b, release both keys, and then immediately press the command key.

Essential Keyboard Shortcuts

Session Operations

Prefix + d: Detach from the current session (leaves it running in the background).
Prefix + $: Rename the current session.
Prefix + s: List and switch between active sessions.



Window (Tab) Operations

Prefix + c: Create a new window.
Prefix + ,: Rename the current window.
Prefix + n / p: Move to the Next or Previous window.
Prefix + 0 through 9: Select window by index number.
Prefix + &: Kill (close) the current window.



Pane Operations

Prefix + %: Split the window vertically (left and right panes).
Prefix + ": Split the window horizontally (top and bottom panes).
Prefix + Arrow Keys: Navigate between panes in the specified direction.
Prefix + x: Kill (close) the active pane.
Prefix + z: Toggle Zoom (maximize the active pane; press again to minimize back).

title: The Ultimate Guide to Tmux: Terminal Multiplexing Made Easy
text:
4. Customizing Tmux
You can customize Tmux configuration by editing the ~/.tmux.conf file. A popular customization is changing the prefix key to Ctrl+a (similar to GNU Screen) and enabling mouse support.
Create or edit your config:
nano ~/.tmux.conf
Add these lines to configure mouse support and custom keybindings:
# Enable mouse click, scroll, and resize support
set -g mouse on

# Remap prefix from 'Ctrl-b' to 'Ctrl-a'
unbind C-b
set-option -g prefix C-a
bind-option C-a send-prefix

# Split panes using | and - instead of % and "
bind | split-window -h
bind - split-window -v
unbind '"'
unbind %

# Improve status bar styling
set -g status-bg black
set -g status-fg white
Apply your changes immediately without restarting Tmux:
tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf

title: Advanced Hyprland: Configuration, Keybinds, & Persistent Workspaces
text:
In our Linux Desktop Guide, we introduced Hyprland as a dynamic tiling Wayland compositor. Unlike traditional desktop environments, Hyprland is configured entirely via plain text files, allowing you to control layouts, windows, animations, and system scripts directly.
In this guide, we will look at how Hyprland’s configuration works, explain tiling resize commands, understand hyprctl, and implement a custom setup to limit your desktop to exactly 10 persistent workspaces using a shell wrapper script.

title: Advanced Hyprland: Configuration, Keybinds, & Persistent Workspaces
text:
1. Modular Configuration Structure
A clean Hyprland setup (like the Illogical Impulse repository) splits configurations into multiple modular files sourced by the main configuration file:
# --- ~/.config/hypr/hyprland.conf ---

# Source external configuration modules
source = ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/general.conf
source = ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/keybinds.conf
source = ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/rules.conf

title: Advanced Hyprland: Configuration, Keybinds, & Persistent Workspaces
text:
2. Deciphering Keybinds and Dispatchers
Keybindings in Hyprland use the bind keyword:
# Syntax: bind = MODIFIERS, KEY, DISPATCHER, ARGUMENTS
bind = $mainMod SHIFT, L, resizeactivetiling, 40
bind = $mainMod SHIFT, H, resizeactivetiling, -40

Breakdown of the command:

$mainMod: Typically mapped to the SUPER key (Windows key).
SHIFT: The secondary modifier key.
L / H: The trigger keys (Right/Left in Vim-like movement).
resizeactivetiling: The dispatcher command. It tells Hyprland to resize the currently active tiled window.
40 / -40: The argument. It resizes the window split border by 40 pixels (positive expands the window, negative shrinks it).

title: Advanced Hyprland: Configuration, Keybinds, & Persistent Workspaces
text:
3. What does hyprctl reload do?
Hyprland provides a command-line interface called hyprctl to control the compositor dynamically.
When you edit configuration files, you can force the system to apply the changes immediately by running:
hyprctl reload
This reloads the configuration modules from disk in real-time. Unlike restarting a session under X11, your Wayland session remains active: none of your running applications, terminals, or browser tabs are closed.

title: Advanced Hyprland: Configuration, Keybinds, & Persistent Workspaces
section: 4. Setup: Limiting to Exactly 10 Persistent Workspaces
text:
4. Setup: Limiting to Exactly 10 Persistent Workspaces
By default, Hyprland creates workspaces dynamically on-demand; if you move your mouse wheel, you can cycle into workspace 11, 12, or higher. To achieve a clean, capped setup of exactly 10 workspaces, follow this three-step procedure:

Step 1: Make Workspaces 1–10 Persistent
Add this to your ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/general.conf (or a dedicated configuration file sourced by your main configuration):
workspace = 1, persistent:true
workspace = 2, persistent:true
workspace = 3, persistent:true
workspace = 4, persistent:true
workspace = 5, persistent:true
workspace = 6, persistent:true
workspace = 7, persistent:true
workspace = 8, persistent:true
workspace = 9, persistent:true
workspace = 10, persistent:true
This forces all 10 workspaces to remain active on your taskbars/bars even if they do not contain any open windows.


Step 2: Create a Workspace Cycle Wrapper Script
The default keybindings cycle infinitely using workspace, e+1. To prevent cycling beyond 10, we will write a script to wrap this action.
Create the script directory and file:
mkdir -p ~/.config/hypr/scripts
Create ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh:
#!/bin/bash
# Usage: workspace-cycle.sh next|prev

# Fetch the active workspace ID using hyprctl JSON output
CURRENT=$(hyprctl activeworkspace -j | jq '.id')

# Calculate the target workspace index (bounded between 1 and 10)
if [[ "$1" == "next" ]]; then
    TARGET=$(( CURRENT < 10 ? CURRENT + 1 : 1 ))
else
    TARGET=$(( CURRENT > 1 ? CURRENT - 1 : 10 ))
fi

# Dispatch the transition to the compositor
hyprctl dispatch workspace "$TARGET"
Make the script executable:
chmod +x ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh


Step 3: Replace Binds in keybinds.conf
Open your ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/keybinds.conf and comment out the default wheel-cycling lines:
# Comment out legacy infinite cycling:
# bind = $mainMod, mouse_down, workspace, e+1
# bind = $mainMod, mouse_up, workspace, e-1

# Bind to our wrapper script:
bind = $mainMod, mouse_down, exec, ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh next
bind = $mainMod, mouse_up,   exec, ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh prev

# Or bind to keyboard keys (e.g., arrow keys):
bind = $mainMod, right, exec, ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh next
bind = $mainMod, left,  exec, ~/.config/hypr/scripts/workspace-cycle.sh prev


Step 4: Audit and Apply
Verify if any other infinite cycling commands exist in your files:
grep 'workspace,' ~/.config/hypr/hyprland/keybinds.conf | grep -v '^#'
Finally, reload the compositor to apply your changes:
hyprctl reload
For a detailed analysis of how this shell cycle script works line-by-line, see the Scripting Fundamentals Guide.

title: Chekhov Reading Guide: ‘Верочка’ (Verochka)
text:
Anton Chekhov’s “Верочка” (Verochka), published in 1887, explores one of his most recurring themes: the tragic inability of people to communicate, step outside their intellectualized isolation, and return sincere emotional vulnerability.
The story follows Ivan Alekseevich Ognev, a statistics researcher from St. Petersburg, who has spent the spring and summer at the rural estate of the Kuznetsov family collecting data. On the eve of his departure, the host’s daughter, Vera (Verochka), walks with him to the edge of the forest and confesses her love for him. Stunned and emotionally paralyzed by his own clinical, bookish detachment, Ognev is unable to feel or offer anything in response.

Иван Алексеевич Огнев помнит, как в тот августовский вечер он со звоном отворил стеклянную дверь и вышел на террасу. На нем была тогда легкая крылатка и широкополая соломенная шляпа, та самая, которая вместе с ботфортами валяется теперь в пыли под кроватью. В одной руке он держал большую вязку книг и тетрадей, в другой — толстую, суковатую палку.



Ботфортами (Botfortami): Jackboots or high thigh-riding boots.
Ботфортами (Botfortami): Jackboots or high thigh-riding boots.
Крылатка (Krylatka): A sleeveless cloak with a cape popular among Russian intellectuals in the 19th century.

За дверью, освещая ему путь лампой, стоял хозяин дома, Кузнецов, лысый старик с длинной седой бородой и в белом, как снег, пикейном пиджаке. Старик благодушно улыбался и кивал головой.



Пикейном пиджаке (Pikeynom pidzhake): A jacket made of pique fabric (a ribbed cotton fabric popular in summer wear).



Пикейном пиджаке (Pikeynom pidzhake): A jacket made of pique fabric (a ribbed cotton fabric popular in summer wear).


— Прощайте, старче! — крикнул ему Огнев.
Кузнецов поставил лампу на столик и вышел на террасу. Две длинные, узкие тени шагнули через ступени к цветочным клумбам, закачались и уперлись головами в стволы лип.
— Прощайте, голубчик! — сказал хозяин. — Спасибо вам за компанию. Не поминайте лихом… Больше не увидимся. Старуха моя уж на небесах, я тоже недолго заживусь на этом свете. Года два-три, да и аминь…



Аминь (Amin’): Amen / the end.

— Да, — вздохнул Огнев. — Больше не увидимся. Спасибо и вам, Гавриил Петрович, за гостеприимство, ласки и за любовь. Не ожидал я от вас такого радушия… Дай бог вам здоровья и всего хорошего.
Огнев семинарским, певучим голосом, каким обыкновенно благодарят хозяев, заговорил опять о радушии, но почувствовал, что слова выходят банальные и не выражают и десятой доли его признательности. А признателен он был глубоко. Этот лысый старик с его дочерью, Вязья, картошка, прогулки, обеды, долгие разговоры по вечерам — всё это так незаметно вошло в его жизнь, так привязало его к себе, что отъезд казался ему теперь потерей чего-то близкого и дорогого.
Кузнецов, растроганный, обнял Огнева и поцеловал его три раза.



Радушия / радушии (Radushiya / radushii): Cordial hospitality, friendliness, or warmth.



Радушия / радушии (Radushiya / radushii): Cordial hospitality, friendliness, or warmth.


— А где же Вера Гавриловна? — спросил Огнев, оглядываясь.
— Она пошла проводить вас до калитки. Верно, в саду сидит.
— Ну, прощайте же!
Огнев сошел с террасы. Пройдя мимо спящих георгинов и кустов пионов, он наткнулся на Веру. Она стояла около калитки, кутаясь в легкий платок.



Георгинов (Georginov): Dahlias (popular garden flowers).
Пионов (Pionov): Peonies.



Георгинов (Georginov): Dahlias (popular garden flowers).
Пионов (Pionov): Peonies. ::: Ей было теперь двадцать один год.

Верочка была хорошо сложена, имела правильный профиль и красивые вьющиеся волосы. Огневу, который на своем веку мало видел женщин, она казалась красавицей.
— Уезжаю! — говорил он, прощаясь с нею около калитки. — Не поминайте лихом! Спасибо за всё!
Тем же певучим семинарским голосом, каким он беседовал со стариком, так же моргая и подергивая плечами, стал он благодарить Веру за гостеприимство, ласки и радушие.
— О вас писал я матери в каждом письме, — говорил он. — Если бы все такие были, как вы да ваш батька, то не житье было бы на свете, а масленая. У вас вся публика великолепная! Народ всё простой, сердечный, искренний.


Масленая (Maslenaya): Shrovetide / a time of luxury and abundance (from the Russian idiom не всё коту масленица).


— Вы теперь куда едете? — спросила Вера.
— Теперь еду к матери в Орел, побуду у нее недельки две, а там — в Питер на работу.
— А потом?
— Потом? Всю зиму проработаю, а весной опять куда-нибудь в уезд материалы собирать. Ну, будьте счастливы, живите сто лет… не поминайте лихом. Больше не увидимся.
Огнев нагнулся и поцеловал Верочкину руку. Затем в молчаливом волнении он поправил на себе крылатку, взял поудобнее вязку книг, помолчал и сказал:
— Туману-то сколько навалило!
— Да. Вы у нас ничего не забыли?
— Что же? Кажется, ничего…
Несколько секунд Огнев постоял молча, потом неуклюже повернулся к калитке и вышел из сада.
— Постойте, я вас до нашего леса провожу, — сказала Вера, выходя за ним.
Они пошли по дороге. Теперь уж деревья не заслоняли простора и можно было видеть небо и даль. Точно прикрытая вуалью, вся природа пряталась за прозрачную матовую дымку, сквозь которую весело смотрела ее красота; туман, что погуще и побелее, неравномерно ложился около копен и кустов или клочьями бродил через дорогу, жался к земле и как будто старался не заслонять собой простора. Сквозь дымку видна была вся дорога до леса с темными канавами по бокам и с мелкими кустами, которые росли в канавах и мешали бродить туманным клочьям. В полуверсте от калитки темнела полоса кузнецовского леса.


Копен (Kopen): Haystacks or haycocks.




Копен (Kopen): Haystacks or haycocks.


«Зачем она со мной пошла? Ведь ее придется провожать назад!» — подумал Огнев, но, поглядев на профиль Веры, он ласково улыбнулся и сказал:
— Не хочется уезжать в такую хорошую погоду! Вечер настоящий романический, с луной, с тишиной и со всеми онерами. Знаете что, Вера Гавриловна? Живу я на свете 29 лет, но у меня в жизни ни разу романа не было. Во всю жизнь ни одной романической истории, так что с рандеву, с аллеями вздохов и поцелуями я знаком только понаслышке. Ненормально! В городе,


Понаслышке (Ponaslyshke): By hearsay / from rumors rather than personal experience.




Понаслышке (Ponaslyshke): By hearsay / from rumors rather than personal experience. ::: когда сидишь у себя в номере, не замечаешь этого пробела, но тут, на свежем воздухе, он сильно чувствуется… Как-то обидно делается!



Онерами (Onerami): Honors / amenities (from French honneurs).
Рандеву (Randevu): Rendezvous / romantic meeting.


— Отчего же вы так?
— Не знаю. Вероятно, всю жизнь некогда было, а может быть, просто встречаться не приходилось с такими женщинами, которые… Вообще у меня мало знакомых, и я нигде не бываю.
Шагов триста молодые люди прошли молча. Огнев поглядывал на открытую голову и платок Верочки, и в душе его один за другим воскресали весенние и летние дни; то было время, когда вдали от своего серого петербургского номера, наслаждаясь ласками хороших людей, природой и любимым трудом, не успевал он замечать, как утренние зори сменялись вечерними и как один за другим, пророча конец лета, переставали петь сначала соловей, потом перепел, а немного позже коростель… Время летело незаметно, значит, жилось хорошо и легко…


Коростель (Korostel’): Corncrake (a secretive brown bird living in grasslands, known for its loud rasping summer call).




Коростель (Korostel’): Corncrake (a secretive brown bird living in grasslands, known for its loud rasping summer call). ::: Стал он припоминать вслух о том, с какою неохотою он, небогатый, непривычный к движениям и людям, в конце апреля ехал сюда в N-ский уезд, где ожидал встретить скуку, одиночество и равнодушие к статистике, которая, по его мнению, среди наук занимает теперь самое видное место. Приехав апрельским утром в уездный городишко N., он остановился на постоялом дворе старовера Рябухина, где за двугривенный в сутки ему дали светлую и чистую комнату с условием, что курить он будет на улице. Отдохнув и справившись, кто в уезде состоит председателем земской управы, он немедля пошел пешком к Гавриилу Петровичу. Пришлось идти четыре версты роскошными лугами и молодыми рощами. Под облаками, заливая воздух серебряными звуками, дрожали жаворонки, а над зеленеющими пашнями, солидно и чинно взмахивая крыльями, носились грачи.



Уезд / уездных (Uezd / uezdnykh): District / provincial; administrative sub-divisions of pre-revolutionary Russia.
Старовера (Starovera): An Old Believer (a member of the religious group that split from the Russian Orthodox Church in the 17th century).
Земской управы (Zemskoy upravy): Local district administrative board or council.
Уезд / уездных (Uezd / uezdnykh): District / provincial; administrative sub-divisions of pre-revolutionary Russia.
Старовера (Starovera): An Old Believer (a member of the religious group that split from the Russian Orthodox Church in the 17th century).
Земской управы (Zemskoy upravy): Local district administrative board or council.
Двугривенный (Dvigrivenny): A twenty-kopeck coin.
Версты (Versty): Versts (an old Russian unit of distance, equal to about 1.06 kilometers or 0.66 miles).
Грачи (Grachi): Rooks (gregarious black birds of the crow family, highly typical of Russian rural landscapes).
Версты (Versty): Versts (an old Russian unit of distance, equal to about 1.06 kilometers or 0.66 miles).
Грачи (Grachi): Rooks (gregarious black birds of the crow family, highly typical of Russian rural landscapes).


— Хорошо тут у вас! — сказал Огнев, когда они подошли к лесу. — Солнце печет, а в лесу тень, прохлада, и пахнет земляникой. Вы помните, Вера Гавриловна, как мы в первый раз ходили в этот лес собирать ягоды?
Вера остановилась.
— Я хочу вам что-то сказать… — проговорила она. — Только вы не сердитесь и не смейтесь над моей глупостью…
Она подняла глаза на Огнева. Ее лицо было бледно, губы дрожали.
— Видите ли… — сказала она. — Я… я люблю вас.
Огнев от неожиданности вздрогнул. Он почувствовал, как краска ударила ему в лицо, и несколько секунд стоял неподвижно, ошеломленный и смущенный.
— Вера Гавриловна… — пробормотал он. — Вы… вы любите меня?


Ошеломленный (Oshelomlenny): Stunned, dumbfounded, or overwhelmed.




Ошеломленный (Oshelomlenny): Stunned, dumbfounded, or overwhelmed.


— Да… — ответила она тихо. — Я полюбила вас с первого дня, как вы приехали к нам… Вы такой умный, добрый, не похожий на наших уездных молодых людей… Я не могла не полюбить вас.
Огнев глядел на ее бледное, взволнованное лицо, на дрожащие губы, и в душе его не рождалось никакого чувства, кроме недоумения и неловкости. Он не любил Веру. Она была для него милой девушкой, хорошим товарищем по прогулкам, но не более. Мысль о любви или браке никогда не приходила ему в голову.
— Вера Гавриловна, — сказал он наконец, стараясь говорить мягко. — Я… я очень благодарен вам за ваше чувство… Но, поверьте, я не стою его. Я сухой, черствый человек, вся жизнь моя в цифрах и бумажках… Я не умею чувствовать так, как вы… Я не смогу сделать вас счастливой.
Вера слушала его, опустив голову. Слезы медленно покатились по ее щекам.
— Я знаю… — прошептала она. — Вы не любите меня… Вы уезжаете в свой Петербург… Но мне хотелось сказать вам это… чтобы вы знали…
Она круто повернулась и быстро пошла назад по дороге к дому. Ее фигура в светлом платке быстро удалялась, тая в тумане.
Огнев постоял немного, глядя ей вслед, потом повернулся и пошел к станции. На душе у него было тяжело и скверно. Он чувствовал себя виноватым в том, что не мог ответить на искреннее, чистое чувство Верочки, и в то же время понимал, что насильно заставить себя полюбить невозможно.
«Почему же я не люблю ее? — думал он, шагая по лесной тропинке. — Она красивая, умная, добрая… Другой на моем месте был бы счастлив… А я стою как пень… Очевидно, книжная жизнь, статистика и одиночество совсем иссушили мою душу…»
Он шел всё быстрее, стараясь заглушить неприятные мысли, но образ Верочки в светлом платке, уходящей в туман, еще долго стоял перед его глазами.

title: JSON Wrangling: Mastering jq and Programmatic Parsing
text:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the lightweight, text-based standard for data exchange on the modern web. From web APIs and configurations to database storage, almost every developer works with JSON daily.
However, viewing, filtering, and parsing JSON can be challenging, especially in shell environments. This guide explains how to master JSON data wrangling using the command-line utility jq, and demonstrates how to parse and serialize JSON programmatically in Python, JavaScript/Node.js, and Rust.


1. What is JSON?
JSON is structured as a collection of key-value pairs (Objects) and ordered lists (Arrays). It supports six primitive and structured types:

String: Unicode characters enclosed in double quotes (e.g., "username").
Number: Double-precision float (e.g., 42 or 3.1415).
Boolean: true or false.
Null: Represents an empty value (null).
Object: An unordered set of key-value pairs wrapped in curly braces ({}).
Array: An ordered collection of values wrapped in brackets ([]).

Example JSON structure (data.json):
{
  "project": "quarto-writing",
  "active": true,
  "stars": 128,
  "maintainers": [
    {"name": "Igor", "role": "Lead"},
    {"name": "Sarah", "role": "Contributor"}
  ],
  "config": {
    "port": 8080,
    "env": "production"
  }
}



2. Command-Line Processing with jq
jq is a lightweight, flexible command-line JSON processor. It functions like sed or awk but is specifically designed to understand JSON hierarchies.

Pretty Printing and Identity
The simplest filter is ., which takes the input and prints it back as formatted (pretty-printed), colorized JSON:
jq . data.json


Extracting Key Values
You can reference keys using dot-notation:
# Get the project name
jq '.project' data.json  # Output: "quarto-writing"

# Get the port inside the config object
jq '.config.port' data.json  # Output: 8080


Extracting Raw Strings (-r or --raw-output)
By default, jq outputs valid JSON (meaning strings are enclosed in double quotes). To output the raw text directly (ideal for storing in shell variables), use the -r flag:
PROJECT=$(jq -r '.project' data.json)
echo "Deploying $PROJECT..."


Iterating Over Arrays
Use .[] to extract elements from an array:
# Print each maintainer object
jq '.maintainers[]' data.json

# Print only the names of all maintainers
jq '.maintainers[].name' data.json
# Output:
# "Igor"
# "Sarah"


Filtering and Selection (select)
You can use conditionals to filter elements out of an array:
# Example JSON array of users
# [{"name": "Alice", "age": 22}, {"name": "Bob", "age": 30}]
cat users.json | jq '.[] | select(.age >= 25)'
# Output: {"name": "Bob", "age": 30}


Creating New Shapes (Object Reconstruction)
You can map elements into completely new JSON shapes:
jq '.maintainers[] | {user: .name, is_lead: (.role == "Lead")}' data.json
# Output:
# { "user": "Igor", "is_lead": true }
# { "user": "Sarah", "is_lead": false }




3. Programmatic JSON Parsing by Language
While jq is excellent for shell scripts and quick investigations, production applications parse JSON programmatically. Here is how three major languages handle it:

Python (json module)
Python has built-in support for JSON, parsing it directly into standard dictionary and list types.
import json

# JSON String
json_string = '{"name": "Igor", "age": 30, "languages": ["Python", "Rust"]}'

# 1. Deserialize (JSON string -> Python dict)
data = json.loads(json_string)
print(f"Name: {data['name']}, Primary Language: {data['languages'][0]}")

# Modify dict
data["active"] = True

# 2. Serialize (Python dict -> JSON string)
updated_json_string = json.dumps(data, indent=2)
print(updated_json_string)


JavaScript / Node.js
JSON is natively integrated into JavaScript, sharing syntax directly with JS objects.
// JSON String
const jsonString = '{"name": "Sarah", "role": "Contributor", "stars": 5}';

// 1. Deserialize (JSON string -> JS Object)
const data = JSON.parse(jsonString);
console.log(`User: ${data.name}, Role: ${data.role}`);

// Modify Object
data.stars += 1;

// 2. Serialize (JS Object -> JSON string)
const updatedJsonString = JSON.stringify(data, null, 2);
console.log(updatedJsonString);


Rust (serde and serde_json crates)
Rust enforces type safety. The industry standard is serde (Serialization/Deserialization), which compiles fast, type-safe structures mapping directly to JSON.
In Cargo.toml:
[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1.0"
In main.rs:
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Debug)]
struct User {
    name: String,
    age: u32,
    languages: Vec<String>,
}

fn main() {
    let json_data = r#"
        {
            "name": "Igor",
            "age": 30,
            "languages": ["Rust", "Python"]
        }
    "#;

    // 1. Deserialize (JSON string -> Rust Struct)
    let user: User = serde_json::from_str(json_data).unwrap();
    println!("Parsed Struct: {:?}", user);
    println!("User Name: {}", user.name);

    // 2. Serialize (Rust Struct -> JSON string)
    let serialized = serde_json::to_string_pretty(&user).unwrap();
    println!("Serialized JSON:\n{}", serialized);
}




4. Conclusion & Quick Reference
For developers, standardizing tools and habits around JSON increases efficiency: * Use jq in terminal pipes to inspect API returns (curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/igor-kan/quarto-writing | jq .stars_count). * Use json.loads/json.dumps in Python for quick scripting. * Define strict structs with serde in Rust to enforce data integrity.

title: Bilingual Reading Guide: ‘Great Expectations’ Chapter I
text:
Charles Dickens’s Great Expectations (1861) is a classic Victorian novel following Pip, an orphaned boy living in the coastal marshes of Kent, England. The novel opens in a chilly, overgrown churchyard where Pip is visiting the graves of his parents and brothers. Suddenly, an escaped convict, Magwitch, jumps out from behind the tombstones, grabs Pip, and threatens him to bring a file and food.



Great Expectations



My father’s family name being Pirrip, and my Christian name Philip, my infant tongue could make of both names nothing longer or more explicit than Pip. So, I called myself Pip, and came to be called Pip.



Christian name: A first name given at birth or baptism, distinct from the family surname.
Explicit: Clear, detailed, and leaving no room for confusion or doubt.

I give Pirrip as my father’s family name, on the authority of his tombstone and my sister,—Mrs. Joe Gargery, who married the blacksmith. As I never saw my father or my mother, and never saw any likeness of either of them (for their days were long before the days of photographs), my first fancies regarding what they were like were unreasonably derived from their tombstones. The shape of the letters on my father’s, gave me an odd idea that he was a square, stout, dark man, with curly black hair. From the character and turn of the inscription, “Also Georgiana Wife of the Above,” I drew a childish conclusion that my mother was freckled and sickly. To five little stone lozenges, each about a foot and a half long, which were arranged in a neat row beside their grave, and were sacred to the memory of five little brothers of mine,—who gave up trying to get a living, exceedingly early in that universal struggle,—I am indebted for a belief I religiously entertained that they had all been born on their backs with their hands in their trousers-pockets, and had never taken them out in this state of existence.



Likeness: A portrait, drawing, image, or physical representation of a person.
Unreasonably: Without good reason, sense, or logic.
Stout: Somewhat fat, heavy, or heavily built.
Lozenges: Diamond-shaped blocks or flat tablets. In Victorian times, small diamond-shaped gravestones or flat stone slabs were sometimes used for infants.

Ours was the marsh country, down by the river, within, as the river wound, twenty miles of the sea. My first most vivid and broad impression of the identity of things seems to me to have been gained on a memorable raw afternoon towards evening. At such a time I found out for certain that this bleak place overgrown with nettles was the churchyard; and that Philip Pirrip, late of this parish, and also Georgiana wife of the above, were dead and buried; and that Alexander, Bartholomew, Abraham, Tobias, and Roger, infant children of the aforesaid, were also dead and buried; and that the dark flat wilderness beyond the churchyard, intersected with dikes and mounds and gates, with scattered cattle feeding on it, was the marshes; and that the low leaden line beyond was the river; and that the distant savage lair from which the wind was rushing was the sea; and that the small bundle of shivers growing afraid of it all and beginning to cry, was Pip.



Nettles: Wild, weed-like plants covered in stinging hairs that inject chemicals causing a painful itch when touched.
Aforesaid: Mentioned previously or earlier in the document or text.
Wilderness: An uncultivated, wild, and uninhabited region.
Dikes: Drainage ditches or low walls constructed to control water levels in marshy or low-lying coastal areas.

“Hold your noise!” cried a terrible voice, as a man started up from among the graves at the side of the church porch. “Keep still, you little devil, or I’ll cut your throat!”
A fearful man, all in coarse grey, with a great iron on his leg. A man with no hat, and with broken shoes, and with an old rag tied round his head. A man who had been soaked in water, and smothered in mud, and lamed by stones, and cut by flints, and stung by nettles, and torn by briars; who limped, and shivered, and glared, and growled; and whose teeth chattered in his head as he seized me by the chin.



Fearful: In old/Victorian English usage, this means causing fear or frightening (rather than feeling afraid).
Smothered: Covered thickly or completely wrapped in something (here, covered completely in wet mud).
Flints: Hard, grey chunks of stone historically used to make tools or strike sparks for fires.
Briars: Thorny wild shrubs or bushes (like wild rose bushes or brambles).

“Oh! Don’t cut my throat, sir,” I pleaded in terror. “Pray don’t do it, sir.”
“Tell us your name!” said the man. “Quick!”
“Pip, sir.”
“Once more,” said the man, staring at me. “Give it mouth!”
“Pip. Pip, sir.”
“Show us where you live,” said the man. “Pint out the place!”



Pleaded: Begged or made an emotional appeal to someone.

I pointed to where our village lay, on the flat in-shore among the alder-trees and pollards, a mile or more from the church.



Pollards: Trees whose top branches have been cut back to encourage a dense head of new foliage and branches, often near waterways.

The man, after looking at me for a moment, turned me upside down, and emptied my pockets. There was nothing in them but a piece of bread. When the church came to itself,—for he was so sudden and strong that he made it go head over heels before me, and I saw the steeple under my feet,—when the church came to itself, I say, I was seated on a high tombstone, trembling while he ate the bread ravenously.
“You young dog,” said the man, licking his lips, “what fat cheeks you ha’ got.”
I believe they were fat, though I was at that time un-dersized for my years, and not strong.



Ravenously: Extremely hungrily; eating fast and with great greed.
Undersized: Smaller than the average size for someone of that age.

“Darn me if I couldn’t eat ’em,” said the man, with a threatening shake of his head, “and if I han’t half a mind to’t!”
I earnestly expressed my hope that he wouldn’t, and held tighter to the tombstone on which he had put me; partly, to keep myself upon it; partly, to keep myself from crying.
“Now lookee here!” said the man. “Where’s your mother?”
“There, sir!” said I.
He started, made a short run, and stopped and looked over his shoulder.
“There, sir!” I timidly explained. “Also Georgiana. That’s my mother.”
“Oh!” said he, coming back. “And is that your father alonger your mother?”
“Yes, sir,” said I; “him too; late of this parish.”
“Ha!” he muttered then, considering. “Who d’ye live with,—supposin’ you’re kindly let to live, which I han’t made up my mind about?”
“My sister, sir,—Mrs. Joe Gargery,—wife of Joe Gargery, the blacksmith, sir.”
“Blacksmith, eh?” said he. And looked down at his leg.
After darkly looking at his leg and me several times, he came closer to my tombstone, took me by both arms, and tilted me back as far as he could hold me; so that his eyes looked most powerfully down into mine, and mine looked most helplessly up into his.



Tilted: Slanted, leaned, or tipped to one side.

“Now lookee here,” he said, “the question being whether you’re to be let to live. You know what a file is?”
“Yes, sir.”
“And you know what wittles is?”
“Yes, sir.”



Wittles: Pip’s spelling of the word victuals (pronounced vit-tles), which is an archaic word meaning food or provisions.

After each question he tilted me over a little more, so as to give me a greater sense of helplessness and danger.
“You get me a file.” He tilted me again. “And you get me wittles.” He tilted me again. “You bring ’em both to me.” He tilted me again. “Or I’ll have your heart and liver out.” He tilted me again.
I was dreadfully frightened, and so giddy that I clung to him with both hands, and said, “If you would kindly please to let me keep upright, sir, perhaps I shouldn’t be sick, and perhaps I could attend more.”
He gave me a most tremendous dip and roll, so that the church jumped over its own weathercock. Then, he held me by the arms, in an upright position on the top of the stone, and went on in these fearful terms:—



Giddy: Dizzy or lightheaded, feeling as if everything is spinning around.
Weathercock: A wind vane shaped like a rooster, placed on top of a church steeple to show the wind direction.

“You bring me, to-morrow morning early, that file and them wittles. You bring the lot to me, at that old Battery over yonder. You do it, and you never dare to say a word or dare to make a sign concerning your having seen such a person as me, or any person sumever, and you shall be let to live. You fail, or you go from my words in any partickler, no matter how small it is, and your heart and your liver shall be tore out, roasted, and ate. Now, I ain’t alone, as you may think I am. There’s a young man hid with me, in comparison with which young man I am a Angel. That young man hears the words I speak. That young man has a secret way pecooliar to himself, of getting at a boy, and at his heart, and at his liver. It is in wain for a boy to attempt to hide himself from that young man. A boy may lock his door, may be warm in bed, may tuck himself up, may draw the clothes over his head, may think himself comfortable and safe, but that young man will softly creep and creep his way to him and tear him open. I am a keeping that young man from harming of you at the present moment, with great difficulty. I find it wery hard to hold that young man off of your inside. Now, what do you say?”



Battery: A small, local military fortification containing artillery guns, usually positioned along coasts or rivers to defend against French ships during the Napoleonic Wars.
Sumever: An old dialect variant or spelling of “soever” (e.g. whatsoever or whomsoever).
In wain: Non-standard phonetic spelling of “in vain” (meaning uselessly or without success), representing the convict’s Cockney accent (swapping ‘v’ and ‘w’).

I said that I would get him the file, and I would get him what broken bits of food I could, and I would come to him at the Battery, early in the morning.
“Say Lord strike you dead if you don’t!” said the man.
I said so, and he took me down.
“Now,” he pursued, “you remember what you’ve undertook, and you remember that young man, and you get home!”
“Goo-good night, sir,” I faltered.



Faltered: Spoke in a hesitant, weak, or trembling voice due to fear or nervousness.

“Much of that!” said he, glancing about him over the cold wet flat. “I wish I was a frog. Or a eel!”
At the same time, he hugged his shuddering body in both his arms,—clasping himself, as if to hold himself together,—and limped towards the low church wall. As I saw him go, picking his way among the nettles, and among the brambles that bound the green mounds, he looked in my young eyes as if he were eluding the hands of the dead people, stretching up cautiously out of their graves, to get a twist upon his ankle and pull him in.



Eluding: Escaping from or avoiding, especially by quickness or cleverness.

When he came to the low church wall, he got over it, like a man whose legs were numbed and stiff, and then turned round to look for me. When I saw him turning, I set my face towards home, and made the best use of my legs. But presently I looked over my shoulder, and saw him going on again towards the river, still hugging himself in both arms, and picking his way with his sore feet among the great stones dropped into the marshes here and there, for stepping-places when the rains were heavy or the tide was in.



Numbed: Deprived of physical feeling or sensation, usually due to extreme cold.

The marshes were just a long black horizontal line then, as I stopped to look after him; and the river was just another horizontal line, not nearly so broad nor yet so black; and the sky was just a row of long angry red lines and dense black lines intermixed. On the edge of the river I could faintly make out the only two black things in all the prospect that seemed to be standing upright; one of these was the beacon by which the sailors steered,—like an unhooped cask upon a pole,—an ugly thing when you were near it; the other, a gibbet, with some chains hanging to it which had once held a pirate. The man was limping on towards this latter, as if he were the pirate come to life, and come down, and going back to hook himself up again. It gave me a terrible turn when I thought so; and as I saw the cattle lifting their heads to gaze after him, I wondered whether they thought so too. I looked all round for the horrible young man, and could see no signs of him. But now I was frightened again, and ran home without stopping.






Beacon: A signaling light, flag, or structural landmark used to guide ships or warn of danger near a river or coastline.
Unhooped cask: A barrel whose metal or wooden hoops (which hold the vertical wooden planks together) have broken off, leaving it loose or falling apart.
Gibbet: A wooden gallows structure used to hang and display the bodies of executed criminals (like pirates) in metal cages or chains as a public warning.
Terrible turn: A sudden, frightening shock or scare.

title: The Mind of the Emperor: Napoleon Bonaparte’s Habits, Reading, and Work Ethic
text:
To the popular imagination, Napoleon Bonaparte (15 August 1769 – 5 May 1821) is remembered primarily as a military genius, a master tactician, and the conqueror of Europe.
However, his military victories were only one facet of a deeply complex, hyper-active intellect. Napoleon was first and foremost an intellectual, a reformer, and an insatiable consumer of knowledge.
His rise from a minor Corsican noble to Emperor of the French was fueled not just by ambition, but by a rigorous self-education, an extraordinary cognitive framework, a legendary work ethic, and a lifelong devotion to reading and writing.
This article explores the private mind of Napoleon: his intense work habits, his structured reading systems, his writing projects, and the mental architecture that allowed him to govern millions of citizens while simultaneously conducting complex military campaigns.

title: The Mind of the Emperor: Napoleon Bonaparte’s Habits, Reading, and Work Ethic
text:
To the popular imagination, Napoleon Bonaparte (15 August 1769 – 5 May 1821) is remembered primarily as a military genius, a master tactician, and the conqueror of Europe.
However, his military victories were only one facet of a deeply complex, hyper-active intellect. Napoleon was first and foremost an intellectual, a reformer, and an insatiable consumer of knowledge.
His rise from a minor Corsican noble to Emperor of the French was fueled not just by ambition, but by a rigorous self-education, an extraordinary cognitive framework, a legendary work ethic, and a lifelong devotion to reading and writing.
This article explores the private mind of Napoleon: his intense work habits, his structured reading systems, his writing projects, and the mental architecture that allowed him to govern millions of citizens while simultaneously conducting complex military campaigns.

title: The Mind of the Emperor: Napoleon Bonaparte’s Habits, Reading, and Work Ethic
section: 1. The Insatiable Reader: Napoleon’s Literary World
text:
1. The Insatiable Reader: Napoleon’s Literary World
From his early childhood in Ajaccio, Corsica, and his lonely school days at the military academy of Brienne-le-Château, Napoleon was a bookworm. While his peers played outside, he retreated to the library, immersing himself in history, mathematics, and geography.

A. The Traveling Library (La Bibliothèque Portative)
Napoleon could not function without books. Wherever he went—whether campaigning in the deserts of Egypt, the snows of Russia, or the palace of Saint-Cloud—he brought a massive library with him.
He commissioned a specialized “traveling library” (bibliothèque portative). Hundreds of books were bound in thin leather, stripped of blank margins to save weight, and packed into custom-designed oak chests lined with green velvet. When he traveled in his carriage, he would read constantly, throwing books out of the window once he had finished them.
In 1808, frustrated by the limitations of standard book sizes, Napoleon instructed his librarian, Antoine-Alexandre Barbier, to design a mobile library of 1,000 volumes printed in a compact 12mo format, specifically divided into: * 40 volumes on religion * 40 volumes of drama * 40 volumes of poetry * 60 volumes of novels * 60 volumes of history * The remainder containing memoirs, biography, and geography


B. What Napoleon Read
Napoleon’s reading preferences reveal his pragmatic approach to knowledge. He read to learn, to govern, and to understand the psychology of the nations he conquered.

The Classics: He was obsessed with antiquity. He read Plutarch’s Parallel Lives repeatedly, drawing inspiration from the leadership of Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar, and Lycurgus. He read Homer’s Iliad and Virgil’s Aeneid.
Political Philosophy: In his youth, he devoured the works of Jean-Jacques Rousseau (particularly The Social Contract), Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws, and John Locke. While he later grew cynical of abstract “ideologues,” their concepts of legal equality and state structure heavily influenced his reforms.
Science and Mathematics: Unlike many contemporary leaders who were educated purely in the humanities, Napoleon was a mathematician. He read treatises on geometry, military engineering, physics, and chemistry.
Literature and Poetry: His favorite work of fiction was Goethe’s The Sorrows of Young Werther, which he claimed to have read seven times. During his meeting with Goethe in Erfurt in 1808, the two spent hours discussing the novel’s structure. He was also a passionate admirer of the pseudo-ancient Celtic poetry of Ossian (compiled by James Macpherson), carrying a copy with him on his campaigns.

title: The Mind of the Emperor: Napoleon Bonaparte’s Habits, Reading, and Work Ethic
text:
2. Work Ethic and Cognitive Systems
Napoleon’s ability to manage a vast empire and direct multiple armies simultaneously was the result of a highly disciplined mind and a work ethic that pushed the boundaries of human endurance.

A. The “Drawers of the Mind”
Napoleon possessed a rare capacity for deep focus. He explained his cognitive organization using the metaphor of a chest of drawers:

“Different subjects and different affairs are arranged in my head as in a cupboard. When I wish to interrupt one train of thought, I close its drawer and open another. They do not mix, and they never fatigue or embarrass me. When I want to sleep, I close all the drawers, and I am fast asleep.”

This mental compartmentalization allowed him to shift from drafting the civil code to planning the logistics of an artillery division within minutes, giving each task his undivided attention.


B. Sleep Habits and Daily Routine
Napoleon’s sleep habits were irregular and highly efficient. * The 4-Hour Sleep Cycle: He rarely slept for more than three or four consecutive hours. He typically retired around 10:00 PM, woke up at 2:00 AM or 3:00 AM when his mind was freshest, worked for several hours, and then took a short bath or a catnap in the afternoon. * Catnaps: Napoleon possessed the ability to fall asleep instantly on command. During battles, he would lay down his cloak, sleep for ten to fifteen minutes amidst the noise of artillery, and wake up fully alert. * The Early Morning Working Hours: He believed that the early hours of the morning were the most productive. He would review administrative reports, finance accounts, and foreign intelligence while the palace was completely silent.


C. Dictation and the Army of Secretaries
Napoleon’s thoughts moved faster than ink could flow. He did not write his official correspondence or decrees by hand; instead, he dictated them. * Simultaneous Dictation: He famously walked pacing back and forth in his study, dictating to three or four secretaries at the same time. Each secretary would write down a different letter, and Napoleon would rotate between them without losing his train of thought. * Speed Requirements: His secretaries had to develop shorthand codes. If a secretary asked him to repeat a sentence, Napoleon would grow furious, stating that his thoughts were a flowing stream that could not be interrupted. * Logistical Attention to Detail: He personally reviewed the smallest administrative details. He checked the prices of bread for his troops, the number of horses in reserve, the condition of boots, and the exact budgets of provincial hospitals. He believed that control over details was the foundation of strategic success.

title: The Mind of the Emperor: Napoleon Bonaparte’s Habits, Reading, and Work Ethic
text:
3. What Napoleon Wrote
Napoleon was a prolific writer throughout his life, transitioning from romantic prose in his youth to administrative genius in his prime, and finally to self-mythologizing memoirs in exile.

A. Romantic Novelist: Clisson et Eugénie
In 1795, as a frustrated 26-year-old artillery officer, Napoleon wrote a short romantic novella titled “Clisson et Eugénie”. * The Plot: The story is a thinly veiled autobiography reflecting his real-life romance with Désirée Clary (who later married Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte and became Queen of Sweden). The protagonist, Clisson, is a brilliant military officer who retreats to the countryside, falls in love with Eugénie, but is eventually called back to war, where he dies heroically after discovering Eugénie’s infidelity. * The Style: Written in the sentimental, melancholy style of Rousseau, the novella showcases a young Napoleon wrestling with themes of honor, love, isolation, and disillusionment.


B. The Imperial Correspondence
The sheer volume of Napoleon’s written output is staggering. The Fondation Napoléon has cataloged over 33,000 surviving letters dictated or written by him. * The Scope: His letters cover everything from passionate, codependent love letters to Joséphine de Beauharnais during the Italian Campaign, to micro-managing instructions to his brothers whom he placed on European thrones, to detailed treaties. * The Tone: His military letters are terse, imperious, and direct. His letters to Joséphine, by contrast, are raw, emotionally volatile, and deeply intimate, revealing a highly passionate temperament.


C. The Exile Memoirs: Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène
Following his defeat at Waterloo in 1815, Napoleon was exiled to the remote South Atlantic island of Saint Helena. With no battles left to fight, he fought his final war on paper, aiming to shape his historical legacy.

The Dictations: Over several years, Napoleon dictated his memoirs, reflections, and historical justifications to his companion in exile, Emmanuel de Las Cases.
The Legacy Project: The resulting book, the Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène, became an instant bestseller across Europe after Napoleon’s death. In it, he reframed his reign not as a military dictatorship, but as a crusade to spread the liberal ideals of the French Revolution (equality, meritocracy, the rule of law) across a feudal Europe. This work laid the foundation for the political ideology of Bonapartism.

title: The Mind of the Emperor: Napoleon Bonaparte’s Habits, Reading, and Work Ethic
text:
4. Key Learnings and Administrative Legacies
Napoleon’s intellectual habits translated directly into practical governance. He considered his administrative reforms to be more permanent than his military victories:

“My true glory is not to have won forty battles… Waterloo will erase the memory of so many victories. But what nothing will destroy, what will live forever, is my Civil Code.” — Napoleon in exile


The Pillars of his Legacy

The Napoleonic Code (Code Civil des Français): Introduced in 1804, this unified system of civil law replaced the chaotic patchwork of feudal laws. It established the equality of all citizens before the law, protected property rights, codified religious freedom, and abolished feudal privileges.
Meritocracy and the Lycées: Napoleon reformed French education by establishing the lycées (selective secondary schools) designed to train a class of civil servants and military officers based on intellectual merit rather than aristocratic birth.
The Egyptian Expedition (1798): When Napoleon invaded Egypt, he did not just take soldiers; he took a “Commission of Sciences and Arts” consisting of 167 scientists, mathematicians, engineers, cartographers, and artists (the savants). This expedition led to:

The mapping of Egypt’s topography and ancient monuments.
The discovery of the Rosetta Stone, which allowed Jean-François Champollion to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs.
The publication of the multi-volume Description de l’Égypte, which effectively founded the modern discipline of Egyptology.

title: Chekhov Reading Guide: ‘Дома’ (Home)
text:
