title: Handling Hyprland API Updates & Breaking Config Changes
text:
Hyprland is a dynamically evolving Wayland compositor. Because it is under active development, its configuration API updates frequently. New versions often deprecate or reorganize configuration options, which can lead to startup warnings, errors, or broken keybinds in popular community configuration presets like Illogical Impulse or other custom rices.
In this guide, we will break down several major breaking changes in recent Hyprland releases, explain what the removed or modified options did, and show you how to patch your configuration files.

title: Handling Hyprland API Updates & Breaking Config Changes
section: 1. The Removal of misc:vfr (Variable Frame Rate)
text:
1. The Removal of misc:vfr (Variable Frame Rate)
In older versions of Hyprland, you would commonly see this line in general.conf or hyprland.conf:
misc {
    vfr = true
}

What did VFR do?
VFR (Variable Frame Rate) allows the display compositor to pause rendering when nothing on the screen is moving or changing. Instead of constantly drawing 60, 120, or 144 frames per second (which consumes GPU cycles and battery power), the compositor only refreshes the screen when there is movement (e.g., cursor motion, video playback, typing).


The Change
Hyprland has completely integrated and automated frame timing. As a result, the vfr configuration parameter was removed from the misc {} block entirely. If you have vfr = true or vfr = false in your configuration, Hyprland will output a red warning bar on startup:

[Config Error] No such field: vfr



The Fix
Simply remove the vfr line from your config file, or comment it out:
misc {
    # vfr = true # Deprecated: Hyprland handles VFR automatically now
}

title: Handling Hyprland API Updates & Breaking Config Changes
text:
2. Reorganization of Shadows (decoration:shadow:ignore_window)
Historically, window shadows were defined directly inside the decoration {} block:
decoration {
    drop_shadow = true
    shadow_range = 4
    shadow_render_power = 3
    col.shadow = rgba(1a1a1aee)
    
    # Deprecated path:
    ignore_window = true 
}

What did ignore_window do?
This option controls how shadows are drawn under semi-transparent windows. * When set to true, the shadow is only rendered around the borders of the window, not underneath it. This prevents the shadow from bleeding through a transparent terminal or application, which would make the background look muddy.


The Change
To organize the growing number of shadow parameters, Hyprland moved all shadow configurations into their own sub-block: decoration:shadow {}. Placing ignore_window directly inside decoration {} now throws configuration errors.


The Fix
Nest the shadow parameters inside a dedicated shadow block:
decoration {
    # Other decoration properties like blur, rounding...

    shadow {
        enabled = true
        range = 4
        render_power = 3
        color = rgba(1a1a1aee)
        ignore_window = true # Correct location
    }
}

title: Handling Hyprland API Updates & Breaking Config Changes
text:
3. Removal of the splitratio Dispatcher
Keybindings in older dotfiles often contained bindings like:
bind = $mainMod, R, splitratio, 0.3

What did splitratio do?
In tiling layouts (like Dwindle or Master), the screen is split between active windows. The splitratio dispatcher allowed you to manually change the dividing ratio of the split window by a specific ratio value, shrinking or expanding the active window relative to its neighbor.


The Change
The splitratio dispatcher was removed. Hyprland now handles active window resizing using more robust dispatchers such as resizeactive or resizeactivetiling.


The Fix
Update your resize keybindings to utilize resizeactive or resizeactivetiling (which take pixel offsets rather than percentage ratios):
# Move split border right (expand active)
bind = $mainMod SHIFT, L, resizeactive, 40 0

# Move split border left (shrink active)
bind = $mainMod SHIFT, H, resizeactive, -40 0

title: Command Line Essentials: Navigating the Shell
text:
The Command Line Interface (CLI) is one of the most powerful tools available to developers and system administrators. While Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs) are convenient, the CLI offers speed, scriptability, and access to powerful system commands that are otherwise unavailable.
This guide provides an overview of the essential commands and concepts needed to confidently navigate the command line.

title: Command Line Essentials: Navigating the Shell
text:
1. Directory Navigation
In the command line, you are always positioned within a specific directory, known as your Current Working Directory (CWD).

pwd (Print Working Directory): Displays the absolute path of your current directory.
ls (List): Lists the contents of the current directory.

ls -l: Detailed list view (permissions, file size, modification date).
ls -a: Show all files (including hidden dotfiles).

cd (Change Directory): Move between folders.

cd /usr/bin: Navigate to an absolute path.
cd ..: Move up one level (parent directory).
cd ~: Jump directly to your home directory.

title: Command Line Essentials: Navigating the Shell
text:
2. File and Folder Manipulation

touch filename: Create an empty file, or update the timestamp of an existing file.
mkdir foldername: Create a new folder.

mkdir -p path/to/folders: Create nested parent directories automatically.

cp source destination: Copy files or directories.

cp -r dir1 dir2: Copy a directory recursively (including all contents).

mv source destination: Move or rename a file or directory.
rm filename: Delete (remove) a file.

rm -rf foldername: Delete a folder and all its contents recursively and forcefully. Use with extreme caution.

title: Command Line Essentials: Navigating the Shell
text:
3. Viewing and Inspecting Files

cat filename: Print the entire content of a file to the terminal screen.
less filename: Open a scrollable viewer for large files. Press q to close.
head -n 10 filename: Output the first 10 lines of a file.
tail -n 10 filename: Output the last 10 lines of a file (useful for monitoring log files).

tail -f /var/log/syslog: Continuously follow updates to a file in real-time.

title: Command Line Essentials: Navigating the Shell
text:
4. Redirecting Output and Piping
Linux treats inputs and outputs as streams. You can redirect these streams to files or pipe them into other commands.

Output Redirection

> (Overwrite): Redirect output to a file, overwriting existing contents.
echo "Hello World" > greetings.txt
>> (Append): Redirect output to a file, appending it to the end of the file.
echo "Another line" >> greetings.txt



Piping (|)
The pipe operator takes the stdout (output) of the command on the left and passes it as stdin (input) to the command on the right.
# List all files and filter for those containing 'config' in their name
ls -la | grep "config"

# Print a log file, filter for errors, and show only the first 5 matches
cat system.log | grep "ERROR" | head -n 5

title: Command Line Essentials: Navigating the Shell
text:
5. Essential Terminal Shortcuts
Save time and avoid typos using these shell keyboard shortcuts: * Tab (Auto-complete): Start typing a filename or command path, and press Tab once to autocomplete. Press twice to list all possibilities. * Ctrl + C: Terminate/kill the currently running process. * Ctrl + Z: Suspend/pause the currently running process (run fg to resume in foreground). * Ctrl + R: Search through your command history. Type characters to find a matching past command. * clear (or Ctrl + L): Clear the terminal screen.

title: The Clinical Eye of Realism: An Introduction to Anton Chekhov
text:
Anton Chekhov (1860–1904) is widely regarded as one of the greatest short story writers and playwrights in world literature. Working during the late Russian Empire, Chekhov pioneered a form of psychological realism that abandoned traditional plots in favor of atmosphere, internal character states, and everyday situations.
A practicing physician throughout his life, Chekhov famously wrote: > “Medicine is my lawful wife, and literature is my mistress. When I get tired of one, I spend the night with the other.”
This medical training gave his writing a unique clinical objectivity; he observed human behavior without judgment, moralizing, or easy sentimentality.

title: The Clinical Eye of Realism: An Introduction to Anton Chekhov
text:
1. Playwriting and Modern Drama
Before Chekhov, late 19th-century theater was dominated by melodrama, neat plot resolutions, and declamatory acting. Chekhov, collaborating with Konstantin Stanislavski at the Moscow Art Theatre, introduced “actionless” drama. In a Chekhov play, nothing extraordinary seems to happen; characters drink tea, complain, and talk, while underneath their lives are falling apart.

The Four Major Plays

The Seagull (1896): Explores artistic ambition, unrequited love, and the conflict between older and younger generations of artists.
Uncle Vanya (1898): Depicts the quiet despair of wasted lives, unrewarded labor, and romantic frustration in the Russian countryside.
Three Sisters (1901): Focuses on the Prozorov sisters, who long to return to the idealized life of Moscow but remain trapped in a provincial military town.
The Cherry Orchard (1904): Captures the decline of the Russian aristocracy and the rise of the merchant class, symbolized by the selling of a family estate.

title: The Clinical Eye of Realism: An Introduction to Anton Chekhov
text:
2. Core Literary Innovations

A. Chekhov’s Gun
A dramatic principle concerning redundancy and plot focus. Chekhov famously wrote: > “If in the first act you have hung a pistol on the wall, then in the following one it should be fired. Otherwise, don’t put it there.”
Every element in a story must be necessary and contribute to the whole.


B. Subtext and Silence
Chekhov was a master of what is left unsaid. Characters rarely express their true feelings directly. Instead, their anxieties, desires, and grief are conveyed through pauses, non-sequiturs, and minor details (a concept that heavily influenced modern writers like Ernest Hemingway and Raymond Carver).


C. Clinical Objectivity
Unlike his contemporaries Leo Tolstoy and Fyodor Dostoevsky, who often used their novels to convey moral or religious philosophies, Chekhov believed the role of the writer was to describe life accurately, not to solve its problems. He wrote: > “The artist should be, not the judge of his characters and their conversations, but only an unbiased witness.”

title: The Clinical Eye of Realism: An Introduction to Anton Chekhov
text:
3. Revolution of the Short Story
Chekhov wrote hundreds of short stories. He pioneered the “zero ending”—refusing to tidy up plots or offer moral resolutions. Stories like The Lady with the Dog, Ward No. 6, and Home (Дома) focus on fleeting moments of realization, leaving the character (and the reader) suspended in uncertainty.

title: Mastering Bash Pipelines & Data Wrangling: Cat, Echo, Grep, and Awk
text:
The Unix philosophy states: “Write programs that do one thing and do it well. Write programs to work together. Write programs to handle text streams, because that is a universal interface.”
In this guide, we will explore the heart of this philosophy: Bash pipelines—which allow us to chain simple utilities together to solve complex data-processing problems. We will cover the mechanics of pipelines and dive deep into four essential tools: cat, echo, grep, and awk.


1. Understanding Bash Pipelines (|)
A pipeline in Bash is created using the vertical bar operator (|). It takes the standard output (stdout) of the command on the left and passes it as standard input (stdin) to the command on the right.
command1 | command2 | command3

How Pipelines Work Under the Hood:

Concurrency: All commands in a pipeline run concurrently (at the same time), not sequentially. The kernel manages the data buffers between processes. If command2 reads slower than command1 writes, command1 is temporarily suspended by the kernel until buffer space becomes available.
Subshells: Each command in a pipeline runs in its own subshell (a separate child process). Consequently, environment variables or directory changes (cd) made inside a pipeline do not affect your parent shell.
Pipeline Exit Codes (PIPESTATUS): By default, the exit code of a pipeline is the exit code of the last command. If command1 fails but command3 succeeds, the overall pipeline returns 0 (success). To see the exit status of each command in the chain, use the Bash environment variable PIPESTATUS:
# Run a pipeline
cat non_existent_file | grep "pattern"
# Inspect exit codes
echo "${PIPESTATUS[0]} ${PIPESTATUS[1]}"  # Prints: 1 1 (both failed)





2. Deep Dive: The Core Utilities

Utility A: cat (Concatenate)
cat is one of the most frequently used commands, designed to read files and print their contents to standard output.

Basic Usage: cat filename.txt
Printing Line Numbers (-n):
cat -n config.conf
Squeezing Empty Lines (-s): Suppresses consecutive empty output lines into a single blank line.
cat -s spacing.txt
Concatenating Multiple Files:
cat part1.log part2.log > combined.log


[!WARNING] Anti-Pattern: Useless Use of Cat (UUOC) Beginners often write cat file.txt | grep "pattern". This spawns a redundant process. Most utilities accept files as arguments directly. Prefer writing: grep "pattern" file.txt




Utility B: echo (Print Text)
echo is a built-in shell utility used to print arguments to standard output.

Basic Usage: echo "Hello, world!"
Suppressing the Newline (-n): By default, echo appends a newline at the end. Use -n to prevent this:
echo -n "Connecting..."
Interpreting Backslash Escapes (-e): Enables interpretation of special characters like tab (\t) and newline (\n).
echo -e "Column1\tColumn2\nValue1\tValue2"


[!TIP] For complex output formatting, prefer the more robust printf utility, which behaves predictably across different Unix shells.




Utility C: grep (Global Regular Expression Print)
grep searches input files (or stream input) for lines matching a specified pattern and prints them.

Case-Insensitive Match (-i):
grep -i "error" server.log
Invert Match (-v): Prints lines that do not match the pattern (highly useful for filtering out noise).
grep -v "DEBUG" server.log
Count Matches (-c): Instead of printing lines, output the count of matching occurrences.
grep -c "ERROR" system.log
Display Line Numbers (-n): Prepends the file line number to each matching line.
grep -n "FATAL" system.log
Recursive Search (-r or -R): Search all files under the specified directory.
grep -rn "TODO" ./src/
Extended Regular Expressions (-E): Interprets pattern as an extended regular expression (equivalent to egrep).
grep -E "(warning|error|critical)" app.log




Utility D: awk (Pattern Scanning and Processing)
awk is not just a command; it is a complete Turing-complete programming language designed for processing columns and structured text.
An awk script consists of patterns and actions:
pattern { action }

Printing Specific Columns: Columns are referenced by $1, $2, etc. $0 represents the entire line.
# Print the username (first column) and shell (seventh column) from /etc/passwd
awk -F ":" '{print $1, $7}' /etc/passwd

Note: The -F flag changes the default field separator (which is whitespace) to a colon (:).

Filtering Rows by Value:
# Print processes where memory usage (column 4) is greater than 5%
ps aux | awk '$4 > 5.0 {print $1, $2, $4, $11}'
Using Built-in Variables:

NR: Number of Records (current line number).
NF: Number of Fields (number of columns in the current line).

# Print the line number followed by the line content
awk '{print NR, $0}' document.txt
Basic Arithmetic & Aggregations:
# Sum the file sizes in bytes (5th column of ls -l)
ls -l | awk '{sum += $5} END {print "Total size:", sum, "bytes"}'





3. Combining Them: Advanced Pipelines
Here are three real-world pipelines showing these tools in action together:

Pipeline A: Analysing Access Logs to Find Top IP Addresses
Extract the IP addresses from an Apache access log, count unique hits, and sort them to find the most active visitors.
cat access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 10

awk '{print $1}' extracts the first column (the client IP address).
sort groups identical IPs together (required for uniq).
uniq -c collapses duplicate lines and counts occurrences.
sort -rn sorts the results numerically (-n) in reverse order (-r) to put high counts at the top.
head -n 10 displays only the top 10 rows.




Pipeline B: Finding and Terminating Specific Processes
Identify running instances of a program (e.g., node) without matching the grep command itself:
ps aux | grep -v "grep" | grep "node" | awk '{print $2}' | xargs kill -9

ps aux lists all active processes.
grep -v "grep" filters out our own search command from the list.
grep "node" filters for lines containing “node”.
awk '{print $2}' prints the second column (the Process ID or PID).
xargs kill -9 passes the PID list as arguments to the kill command.




Pipeline C: Quick File Summary
Verify the number of non-comment, non-empty configuration options in a config file:
grep -v "^#" server.conf | grep -v "^$" | wc -l

grep -v "^#" excludes lines starting with a comment hash.
grep -v "^$" excludes empty lines.
wc -l counts the remaining lines.

title: A Beginner-Friendly Guide to the Nano Text Editor
text:
For users new to the Linux terminal, command-line text editors like Vim or Emacs can feel intimidating due to their modal interfaces and steep learning curves.
GNU Nano is a modeless, lightweight, and easy-to-use text editor that is pre-installed on almost all Linux distributions. What you type is immediately inserted into the file, and a handy shortcut guide is permanently displayed at the bottom of your screen.

title: A Beginner-Friendly Guide to the Nano Text Editor
text:
1. Opening and Creating Files
To create or open a file, run nano followed by the file path:
# Open an existing file or create a new one
nano my_document.txt

# Open a system file with root privileges
sudo nano /etc/hosts

title: A Beginner-Friendly Guide to the Nano Text Editor
text:
2. Essential Shortcuts
In Nano, shortcuts are represented by the caret symbol (^), which denotes the Ctrl key, or M- which denotes the Meta key (usually the Alt key on PCs or Esc key).
Here are the most important shortcuts to know:

File Management

Ctrl + O (Write Out): Save the changes to the file without closing it.
Ctrl + X (Exit): Exit Nano. If you have unsaved changes, it will ask if you want to save (Y or N).



Editing Text

Ctrl + K (Cut): Cut the entire current line of text (like cutting to a clipboard).
Ctrl + U (Uncut): Paste the text that was just cut.
Ctrl + 6 (or Alt + A): Start selecting text. Use arrow keys to select, then Ctrl + K to cut.



Searching and Navigation

Ctrl + W (Where Is): Search for a specific word or string of text.
Ctrl + \ (Replace): Search for a word and replace it with another.
Ctrl + _ (Go to Line): Jump directly to a specific line and column number.
Ctrl + C (Cur Pos): Show current line number, column number, and character count.

title: A Beginner-Friendly Guide to the Nano Text Editor
text:
3. Configuring Nano: The .nanorc File
You can customize Nano’s default behavior by creating a configuration file in your home directory:
nano ~/.nanorc
Add the following options to enable useful features like syntax highlighting, line numbers, and proper indentation:
# Display line numbers on the left
set linenumbers

# Enable smooth scrolling (scrolls line-by-line instead of half-page)
set smooth

# Set tab size to 4 spaces instead of 8
set tabsize 4

# Convert typed tabs into spaces
set tabstospaces

# Enable auto-indentation of new lines
set autoindent

# Enable mouse support (allows clicking to position cursor)
set mouse

# Enable standard syntax highlighting styles
include "/usr/share/nano/*.nanorc"
Once saved, these settings will apply automatically every time you launch Nano.

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
text:
In English, how we ask questions says a lot about our relationship with the listener, the context of the conversation, and our level of politeness.
Compare these two queries: 1. “Where is the bathroom?” 2. “Could you tell me where the bathroom is?”
While both seek the exact same information, the first is a direct question, which can sound abrupt or demanding, especially when speaking to strangers. The second is an indirect question, which softens the request by embedding the question inside a polite introductory phrase.
For English learners, mastering indirect questions is one of the most critical milestones for achieving professional fluency. For native speakers, understanding the subtle syntax of embedded clauses prevents hypercorrections and enhances stylistic clarity.
This guide provides a comprehensive breakdown of direct and indirect questions, highlighting structural rules, tense shifts, punctuation, and advanced stylistic nuances.

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
text:
1. Grammatical Framework: The Golden Rules
When transforming a direct question into an indirect question, you must follow three fundamental grammatical changes.

Rule 1: Use Statement Word Order (No Subject-Verb Inversion)
In direct questions, the subject and the verb are inverted (the verb or auxiliary comes before the subject). In indirect questions, we revert to standard declarative (statement) word order: Subject + Verb.

Direct: Where is (verb) the station (subject)?
Indirect: Can you tell me where the station (subject) is (verb)?

(Incorrect: Can you tell me where is the station?)

Direct: What time does (auxiliary) the meeting (subject) start?
Indirect: Do you know what time the meeting (subject) starts (verb)?

(Incorrect: Do you know what time does the meeting start?)




Rule 2: Omit Auxiliary Verbs (Do, Does, Did)
In direct questions, we use the auxiliary verbs do, does, or did to form questions in the Simple Present and Simple Past. In indirect questions, these auxiliaries are completely dropped, and the main verb must be conjugated to match the subject and tense.

Direct (Present Simple): Where do you live?
Indirect: Could you tell me where you live? (Not: where do you live)
Direct (Present Simple 3rd Person): What does he want?
Indirect: I wonder what he wants. (Verb conjugated with -s; not: what does he want)
Direct (Past Simple): Why did she leave?
Indirect: I don’t know why she left. (Verb conjugated in past tense; not: why did she leave / why she did leave)



Rule 3: Use If or Whether for Yes/No Questions
If a direct question does not begin with a question word (who, what, where, when, why, how), it is a Yes/No question. To make it indirect, you must introduce the embedded clause using if or whether.

Direct: Is she coming to the party?
Indirect: Do you know if she is coming to the party?
Direct: Did you finish the report?
Indirect: Could you let me know whether you finished the report?

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
text:
2. Comparison Across Verb Tenses & Forms
To illustrate how these rules apply systematically, here is an extensive comparison across major English tenses and modal structures.









Tense / Form
Direct Question
Indirect Question (Polite Opening)
Indirect Question (Statement Opening)




Present Simple
“Where is he?”
“Do you know where he is?”
“I am not sure where he is.”


Present Simple (Action)
“How often do you exercise?”
“Could you tell me how often you exercise?”
“I would like to know how often you exercise.”


Present Continuous
“What are they doing?”
“Do you have any idea what they are doing?”
“I want to see what they are doing.”


Past Simple
“Where did you buy that?”
“Would you mind telling me where you bought that?”
“He didn’t mention where he bought that.”


Past Continuous
“Who was she talking to?”
“Can you remember who she was talking to?”
“I was wondering who she was talking to.”


Present Perfect
“Why have they left?”
“Do you know why they have left?”
“It’s unclear why they have left.”


Past Perfect
“What had he prepared?”
“Can you tell me what he had prepared?”
“She didn’t disclose what he had prepared.”


Future (Will)
“When will the package arrive?”
“Do you know when the package will arrive?”
“I was wondering when the package will arrive.”


Future (Going to)
“Who are you going to invite?”
“Could you tell me who you are going to invite?”
“I’m curious who you are going to invite.”


Modal (Should)
“What should we do?”
“Do you have any advice on what we should do?”
“We need to figure out what we should do.”


Modal (Can)
“Where can I park?”
“Could you show me where I can park?”
“I need to find out where I can park.”

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
section: 3. Polite Phrases to Start Indirect Questions
text:
3. Polite Phrases to Start Indirect Questions
The tone of an indirect question is determined by the introductory clause. Here are the most common phrases grouped by usage.

A. Polite Inquiries (Ended with a Question Mark)
Use these when asking a question to a stranger, a colleague, or a customer. * “Could you tell me…” (Very common, polite, and versatile) * “Do you know…” (Slightly more direct, but still polite) * “Do you have any idea…” (Useful when you suspect the person might not know the answer) * “Would you mind telling me…” (Extremely polite; note that if followed by a verb it takes -ing, e.g., “Would you mind telling me what time it is?”) * “Can you remember…” (Used when asking about past events or details)


B. Statement Openings (Ended with a Period)
Use these to express uncertainty, curiosity, or when you are reporting information. * “I was wondering…” (Very soft and polite, commonly used in emails) * “I’d like to know…” (Professional and clear, shows intent) * “I’m not sure…” (Expresses doubt or lack of information) * “I don’t know…” (Simple statement of fact) * “I want to find out…” (Expresses a goal or objective) * “It is not clear…” (Formal, analytical)

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
text:
4. Nuances: Punctuation and “If” vs. “Whether”
Even advanced speakers make mistakes on these two key areas of indirect question usage.

A. Punctuation Rules
Should an indirect question end with a question mark (?) or a period (.)? The rule depends entirely on the introductory clause:

If the introductory clause is a question, the whole sentence ends with a question mark.

Do you know (question) where he lives?
Could you tell me (question) if it’s raining?

If the introductory clause is a statement, the whole sentence ends with a period.

I was wondering (statement) where he lives.
I’d like to know (statement) if it’s raining.




B. If vs. Whether
While if and whether are interchangeable in most yes/no indirect questions, there are subtle differences:

Use “whether” in formal writing: It sounds more professional and academic.

Formal: “The board must decide whether to approve the budget.”

Use “whether” when presenting two explicit options (especially with “or not”):

“I don’t know whether they will accept the offer or not.”
“Could you tell me whether he is arriving by train or plane?”

Use “whether” immediately before an infinitive (to + verb):

“She was debating whether to buy the house.” (You cannot say “if to buy”)

Use “whether” after prepositions:

“We had a discussion about whether we should relocate.” (You cannot say “about if we should”)

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
section: 5. Advanced Stylistic & Syntactic Analyses (For Native & Advanced Speakers)
text:
5. Advanced Stylistic & Syntactic Analyses (For Native & Advanced Speakers)
For fluent and native speakers, indirect questions present interesting syntactic structures, reported speech rules, and common errors to avoid.

A. Fronted Wh-Words vs. Embedded Questions
Consider the difference between these two constructions involving opinion verbs (like think, believe, suppose):

Embedded Wh-clause: “Do you know who that candidate is?”

Here, “who that candidate is” is a noun clause serving as the direct object of the verb “know”.

Fronted Wh-word: “Who do you think that candidate is?”

In sentences with verbs of opinion (think, believe, suppose, imagine), the wh-word is extracted from the embedded clause and moved to the front of the entire sentence.
Incorrect: “Do you think who that candidate is?”




B. Indirect Questions in Reported Speech (Backshifting)
When reporting a question that was asked in the past, the tenses in the indirect question must typically shift backward (backshifting):

Original Direct Question: “Where are you going?” (Present Continuous)
Reported Indirect Question: “She asked me where I was going.” (Past Continuous)
Original Yes/No Question: “Did you see the movie?” (Past Simple)
Reported Indirect Question: “He wanted to know if I had seen the movie.” (Past Perfect)



C. Infinitival Indirect Questions
In English, we can shorten indirect questions when the subject of the introductory clause is the same as the subject of the question. We do this by replacing the subject and auxiliary with a to-infinitive:

“I don’t know what I should do.” \(\rightarrow\) “I don’t know what to do.”
“Could you tell me how I can get there?” \(\rightarrow\) “Could you tell me how to get there?”
“She wasn’t sure whether she should go.” \(\rightarrow\) “She wasn’t sure whether to go.”



D. Hypercorrection and Spoken English Deviations
In informal spoken English, native speakers often apply direct question inversion to indirect clauses. While common in casual speech, this is considered ungrammatical in formal writing.

Casual Speech: “He asked me what was I doing.”
Grammatically Correct: “He asked me what I was doing.”
Casual Speech: “I wonder how did they manage to do that.”
Grammatically Correct: “I wonder how they managed to do that.”

title: Direct and Indirect Questions: The Complete Grammar & Style Guide
text:
6. Practice Exercises & Sentence Transformations
Test your skills by rewriting these direct questions into indirect questions.

Exercise 1: Transform to Indirect (Polite Question form)
Example: “Where is the post office?” \(\rightarrow\) “Could you tell me where the post office is?”

“What time does the bank close?” (Use: Do you know…)
“Is there a vegetarian option on the menu?” (Use: Could you tell me…)
“Why did the project fail?” (Use: Do you have any idea…)
“Where can I find a taxi?” (Use: Would you mind showing me…)
“Will it snow tomorrow?” (Use: Do you know…)



Exercise 2: Transform to Indirect (Statement form)
Example: “Why is she upset?” \(\rightarrow\) “I don’t know why she is upset.”

“How did he solve the puzzle?” (Use: I was wondering…)
“Should we sign the contract?” (Use: We need to decide whether…)
“When are they arriving?” (Use: I’m not sure…)
“Did he receive my email?” (Use: I’d like to find out…)
“Where did I leave my keys?” (Use: I can’t remember…)




Answer Key

Exercise 1

Do you know what time the bank closes? (No “does”, conjugated verb)
Could you tell me if/whether there is a vegetarian option on the menu? (Yes/no question uses if/whether)
Do you have any idea why the project failed? (Past tense main verb, no “did”)
Would you mind showing me where I can find a taxi? (Subject “I” before modal “can”)
Do you know if/whether it will snow tomorrow?



Exercise 2

I was wondering how he solved the puzzle. (Ends with a period)
We need to decide whether to sign the contract. (Or: whether we should sign…)
I’m not sure when they are arriving.
I’d like to find out if/whether he received my email.
I can’t remember where I left my keys.

title: Vim and Neovim Tutorial: Modal Editing & System Clipboard Setup
text:
Vim and its modern extension Neovim are highly efficient, terminal-based modal text editors. Unlike standard text editors, Vim segregates typing text from executing navigation commands by utilizing different “modes.”
In this tutorial, we will cover the core modes, key navigation, essential commands, and how to resolve one of the most common friction points for new users: setting up seamless copy-pasting to and from the system clipboard.

title: Vim and Neovim Tutorial: Modal Editing & System Clipboard Setup
text:
1. The Core Concept: Modal Editing
When you open Vim or Neovim, you start in Normal Mode. You cannot type text immediately; instead, keys on your keyboard act as shortcuts for moving around and editing the file.
There are three primary modes: * Normal Mode (Default): For navigation, deleting, copying, and pasting text. Press Esc to return to this mode from any other mode. * Insert Mode: For writing text. Enter this mode by pressing i (insert before cursor) or a (append after cursor). * Visual Mode: For selecting blocks of text. Enter this mode by pressing v (character-wise) or V (line-wise).

title: Vim and Neovim Tutorial: Modal Editing & System Clipboard Setup
text:
2. Essential Navigation & Commands
All of these commands are executed from Normal Mode.

Navigation (HJKL)
Avoid the arrow keys. Use these keys to keep your fingers on the home row: * h: Move left * j: Move down * k: Move up * l: Move right


Basic Editing Commands

x: Delete character under cursor.
dd: Delete (cut) the entire current line.
yy: Copy (yank) the entire current line.
p: Paste (put) copied text after the cursor.
u: Undo the last action (Ctrl + r to redo).



Command Line Mode (Ex Commands)
Press : to enter command line mode, then type: * :w: Save changes (write). * :q: Quit Vim. * :wq: Save changes and quit (equivalent to :x or ZZ). * :q!: Quit without saving changes.

title: Vim and Neovim Tutorial: Modal Editing & System Clipboard Setup
section: 3. Configuring Copy-Paste to the System Clipboard
text:
3. Configuring Copy-Paste to the System Clipboard
By default, when you copy (yank) text using y or delete text using d, Vim stores it in its internal registers, not your system’s global clipboard. This means you cannot paste yanked text into your web browser or another application.
To bridge this gap, Vim uses special registers: * + represents the system clipboard (global copy/paste). * * represents the primary selection (middle-click paste).

Step 1: Verification
First, verify that your Vim or Neovim installation has clipboard support compiled in.
For Vim, run:
vim --version | grep clipboard
If you see +clipboard or +xterm_clipboard, clipboard integration is supported. If you see -clipboard, you need to install a version of Vim with GUI support (like vim-gtk3 on Ubuntu or gvim on Arch).
For Neovim, clipboard support is handled through external utilities. You must install the appropriate tool for your display server:
# For X11 (Arch Linux / Ubuntu)
sudo pacman -S xclip xsel     # Arch
sudo apt install xclip xsel    # Ubuntu

# For Wayland (Arch Linux / Ubuntu)
sudo pacman -S wl-clipboard   # Arch
sudo apt install wl-clipboard  # Ubuntu


Step 2: Configuring Auto-Clipboard Integration
Rather than typing special keys to access the clipboard registers every time, you can configure Vim/Neovim to automatically route all yanks and deletes directly to the system clipboard.

For Vim:
Edit your ~/.vimrc:
nano ~/.vimrc
Add the following line:
" Automatically sync Vim registers with the system clipboard
set clipboard=unnamedplus


For Neovim:
Edit your configuration file: * If using Lua (~/.config/nvim/init.lua): lua   -- Sync Neovim register with system clipboard   vim.opt.clipboard = "unnamedplus" * If using Vimscript (~/.config/nvim/init.vim): vim   set clipboard=unnamedplus



Step 3: Copying & Pasting Manually (Without configuration)
If you are on a server and don’t want to change your global configuration, you can target the system clipboard register (+) explicitly:

To Copy (Yank) to Clipboard:

Highlight text in Visual Mode (v).
Type: "+y (Double quote, plus sign, yank).

To Paste from Clipboard:

In Normal Mode, place the cursor where you want the text.
Type: "+p (Double quote, plus sign, paste).

title: Advanced Shell Redirection and Network Requests: Mastering curl, tee, and More
text:
Unix-like operating systems are packed with small, single-purpose command-line tools. When combined, these utilities form a highly flexible scripting environment.
In this guide, we will master curl (for making network requests), tee (for splitting output streams), and other core tools like xargs and find that are essential for command-line efficiency.


1. Network Requests with curl
curl (Client URL) is a tool used to transfer data to or from a server using supported protocols (such as HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, etc.). It is widely used for debugging APIs, downloading files, and testing network endpoints.

Making a Basic GET Request
By default, curl prints the response body of a request directly to the terminal screen (stdout):
curl https://api.github.com/zen


Downloading Files (-o and -O)

-o <filename>: Saves the downloaded resource under a custom filename.
curl -o output.html https://example.com
-O (Uppercase O): Saves the file using its remote filename.
curl -O https://releases.ubuntu.com/24.04/ubuntu-24.04-desktop-amd64.iso



Sending POST Requests (-d / --data)
To send data to an endpoint (like a REST API), use the -d flag. This automatically changes the request method from GET to POST:
curl -d '{"username":"admin", "role": "developer"}' \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     https://httpbin.org/post


Custom Headers (-H / --header)
Add custom headers for authentication or content-type specification:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN_HERE" https://api.github.com/user


Following Redirects (-L / --location)
By default, curl does not follow HTTP redirects (301 or 302 status codes). Use -L to follow them automatically:
curl -L http://github.com  # Redirects to https://github.com


Inspecting Headers and Debugging (-I and -v)

-I (Uppercase i): Fetch only the HTTP response headers (GET method becomes HEAD).
curl -I https://example.com
-v (Verbose): Prints complete debug logs including TLS handshakes, request headers, and response status.
curl -v https://example.com





2. Splitting Streams with tee
tee is named after the T-splitter used in plumbing. It reads from standard input (stdin) and writes to both standard output (stdout) and one or more files simultaneously.
flowchart TD
    stdin[Standard Input] --> tee[tee Command]
    tee --> stdout[Standard Output / Terminal]
    tee --> file[File on Disk]
    
    style tee fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px

Basic Usage
Print command output to the screen and save it to a file:
ls -la | tee file_list.txt


Appending Output (-a / --append)
By default, tee overwrites the destination file. Use -a to append text to the end of the file instead:
echo "Session Log Start" | tee -a log.txt


The Classic Sysadmin Trick: Writing with sudo
Standard output redirection (>) is handled by the shell itself, not the command. This means running sudo echo "nameserver 1.1.1.1" > /etc/resolv.conf will fail because your shell does not have permission to write to /etc/resolv.conf, even though the echo command was run with sudo.
To solve this, use tee combined with sudo:
echo "nameserver 1.1.1.1" | sudo tee /etc/resolv.conf
Since tee runs as a process, launching it with sudo gives it permission to write directly to protected system files.




3. Other Essential CLI Commands

Utility A: xargs (Build and Execute Commands)
xargs reads items from standard input (delimited by blanks or newlines) and executes a command using those items as arguments.
# Find all .tmp files and delete them in one go
find . -name "*.tmp" | xargs rm
Why use xargs? If you find 1,000 files, xargs gathers them and runs rm file1 file2 ... file1000 as a single process, rather than launching 1,000 individual rm processes.


Utility B: find (Search Filesystem)
find searches directory trees recursively for files matching specific criteria.
# Find files by name (case-insensitive)
find /home -iname "*.config"

# Find only directories modified in the last 24 hours
find . -type d -mmin -1440


Utility C: tar (Tape Archive)
tar is used to pack or unpack file archives.

Create a Compressed Archive (-czvf):
# c = create, z = gzip compress, v = verbose progress, f = archive file name
tar -czvf backup.tar.gz /path/to/folder
Extract a Compressed Archive (-xzvf):
# x = extract
tar -xzvf backup.tar.gz -C /target/directory





4. Combining the Tools into Pipelines
By combining these utilities, you can write highly efficient one-liners:

Example: Download a JSON payload, pretty-print to terminal, log to disk, and parse out a token
curl -s -d '{"user":"test"}' https://httpbin.org/post | \
  tee request_log.json | \
  jq -r '.json.user'

curl -s fetches the payload silently.
tee request_log.json saves the exact response payload to disk while forwarding it down the pipeline.
jq parses the json and prints the user property raw to stdout.

title: Formal Rules of Syntactic Implication
text:
Syntactic implication utilizes deductive inference rules to transform premise sets into target conclusions. In what is also called a Sequent-style Calculus or Natural Deduction framework, let \(\Gamma\) represent a set of formulas acting as premises (a.k.a. hypotheses), let \(\varphi, \psi, \theta\) represent individual formulas, and let the turnstile symbol \(\vdash\) denote “syntactically derives.”

Basic Proofs (Axioms)
These foundational rules establish the starting points for any formal derivation.

Assumption (\(Assume_{\mathcal{L}}\)): If a formula is already present within your active set of hypotheses, it is derived trivially.
\[\Gamma \vdash \varphi \quad \text{if } \varphi \in \Gamma\]
Equality Reflexivity (\(EqRefl\)): Every valid term is inherently equal to itself.
\[\Gamma \vdash t = t \quad \text{for all } t \in \text{Term}_{\mathcal{L}}\]



Proof Rules (Connectives)
These inference rules dictate how to introduce new logical connectives into a derivation or eliminate existing ones to extract substructures.

Conjunction

Elimination (\(\wedge EL\) and \(\wedge ER\)): If a compound conjunction is derived, either constituent proposition can be extracted individually.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \wedge \psi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \wedge \psi}{\Gamma \vdash \psi}\]
Introduction (\(\wedge I\)): If independent derivations exist for two separate formulas, they can be unified into a single conjunction.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \quad \Gamma \vdash \psi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \wedge \psi}\]



Disjunction

Introduction (\(\vee IL\) and \(\vee IR\)): If a formula is derived, it can be disjoined with any arbitrary proposition while preserving validity.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \vee \psi} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\Gamma \vdash \psi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \vee \psi}\]
Proof by Cases (\(\vee PC\)): If two distinct hypotheses independently derive the identical consequent \(\theta\), then the disjunction of those hypotheses also derives \(\theta\).
\[\frac{\Gamma \cup \{\varphi\} \vdash \theta \quad \Gamma \cup \{\psi\} \vdash \theta}{\Gamma \cup \{\varphi \vee \psi\} \vdash \theta}\]



Implication

Elimination / Modus Ponens (\(\to E\)): If a conditional implication and its operational antecedent are both derived, the consequent necessarily follows.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \to \psi \quad \Gamma \vdash \varphi}{\Gamma \vdash \psi}\]
Introduction / Deduction Theorem (\(\to I\)): If assuming a provisional hypothesis successfully derives a target formula, the overarching implication is established.
\[\frac{\Gamma \cup \{\varphi\} \vdash \psi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi \to \psi}\]



Negation and Contradiction

Proof by Contradiction (\(\neg PC\)): If assuming a hypothesis yields a structural contradiction (deriving both a formula and its explicit negation), the hypothesis is refuted.
\[\frac{\Gamma \cup \{\psi\} \vdash \varphi \quad \Gamma \cup \{\psi\} \vdash \neg \varphi}{\Gamma \vdash \neg \psi}\]
Contradiction Rule / Reductio ad Absurdum (\(Contr\)): If assuming the negation of a proposition yields a logical contradiction, the foundational proposition is affirmed as true.
\[\frac{\Gamma \cup \{\neg \varphi\} \vdash \psi \quad \Gamma \cup \{\neg \varphi\} \vdash \neg \psi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi}\]




Equality Rules

Substitution (\(=Sub\)): If a formula holds true for a specific term \(t\), and an explicit identity mapping establishes that \(t\) equals \(u\), the formula remains valid when \(t\) is replaced by \(u\).
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi^x_t \quad \Gamma \vdash t = u}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi^x_u}\]



Quantifier Rules
Quantifier rules govern the systematic introduction and elimination of operational scope variables across domains.

Existential Quantifiers

Introduction (\(\exists I\)): Proving that a specific instantiated term satisfies a target property confirms that there exists at least one element satisfying that property.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi^x_t}{\Gamma \vdash \exists x \, \varphi}\]
Existential Elimination / Proof (\(\exists P\)): If an arbitrary placeholder \(y\) can derive a conclusion \(\psi\) from an existential statement, the derivation holds universally, provided \(y\) remains unbound within the surrounding context.
\[\Gamma \cup \{\varphi^x_y\} \vdash \psi \quad \Gamma \cup \{\exists x \, \varphi\} \vdash \psi \quad \text{if } y \notin \text{FreeVar}(\Gamma \cup \{\exists x \, \varphi, \psi\})\]



Universal Quantifiers

Elimination (\(\forall E\)): If a property is universally quantified across an entire domain, it holds valid for any specific instantiated term \(t\).
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \forall x \, \varphi}{\Gamma \vdash \varphi^x_t}\]
Introduction (\(\forall I\)): If a property can be derived for a completely arbitrary, unconstrained placeholder \(y\), it is formally established for all elements in the domain.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi^x_y}{\Gamma \vdash \forall x \, \varphi} \quad \text{if } y \notin \text{FreeVar}(\Gamma \cup \{\forall x \, \varphi\})\]




Superset Rule

Monotonicity (\(Super\)): Classical deduction is monotonic. Adding supplementary hypotheses to a valid derivation context never invalidates the previously established conclusion.
\[\frac{\Gamma \vdash \varphi}{\Gamma' \vdash \varphi} \quad \text{if } \Gamma' \supseteq \Gamma\]

title: Chapter 1: Limits and Continuity
text:
The concept of a limit is the fundamental building block of calculus. It formalizes the idea of approaching a specific value.


Suppose \(f(x)\) is defined when \(x\) is near the number \(a\). If we can make the values of \(f(x)\) arbitrarily close to \(L\) (as close to \(L\) as we like) by restricting \(x\) to be sufficiently close to \(a\) (but not equal to \(a\)), we write:
\[ \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \]
This says that “the limit of \(f(x)\), as \(x\) approaches \(a\), equals \(L\).”



Assume that \(c\) is a constant and the limits \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x)\) and \(\lim_{x \to a} g(x)\) exist.

Sum Law: \(\lim_{x \to a} [f(x) + g(x)] = \lim_{x \to a} f(x) + \lim_{x \to a} g(x)\)
Difference Law: \(\lim_{x \to a} [f(x) - g(x)] = \lim_{x \to a} f(x) - \lim_{x \to a} g(x)\)
Constant Multiple Law: \(\lim_{x \to a} [c \cdot f(x)] = c \cdot \lim_{x \to a} f(x)\)
Product Law: \(\lim_{x \to a} [f(x) \cdot g(x)] = \lim_{x \to a} f(x) \cdot \lim_{x \to a} g(x)\)
Quotient Law: \(\lim_{x \to a} \left[ \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \right] = \frac{\lim_{x \to a} f(x)}{\lim_{x \to a} g(x)}\), provided \(\lim_{x \to a} g(x) \neq 0\)




To prove limits rigorously, we use the \(\epsilon-\delta\) definition (which will be explored deeply in Real Analysis).
Definition: Let \(f\) be a function defined on some open interval that contains the number \(a\), except possibly at \(a\) itself. Then we say that the limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches \(a\) is \(L\), and we write \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\), if for every number \(\epsilon > 0\) there is a number \(\delta > 0\) such that:
\[ \text{if } 0 < |x - a| < \delta \text{ then } |f(x) - L| < \epsilon \]



A function is continuous if you can draw its graph without lifting your pen. Mathematically:
A function \(f\) is continuous at a number \(a\) if: \[ \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a) \]
This implies three things: 1. \(f(a)\) is defined. 2. \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x)\) exists. 3. The limit equals the function value at that point.

Assume that \(c\) is a constant and the limits \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x)\) and \(\lim_{x \to a} g(x)\) exist.

Sum Law: \(\lim_{x \to a} [f(x) + g(x)] = \lim_{x \to a} f(x) + \lim_{x \to a} g(x)\)
Difference Law: \(\lim_{x \to a} [f(x) - g(x)] = \lim_{x \to a} f(x) - \lim_{x \to a} g(x)\)
Constant Multiple Law: \(\lim_{x \to a} [c \cdot f(x)] = c \cdot \lim_{x \to a} f(x)\)
Product Law: \(\lim_{x \to a} [f(x) \cdot g(x)] = \lim_{x \to a} f(x) \cdot \lim_{x \to a} g(x)\)
Quotient Law: \(\lim_{x \to a} \left[ \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \right] = \frac{\lim_{x \to a} f(x)}{\lim_{x \to a} g(x)}\), provided \(\lim_{x \to a} g(x) \neq 0\)

title: Chapter 1: Limits and Continuity
text:
To prove limits rigorously, we use the \(\epsilon-\delta\) definition (which will be explored deeply in Real Analysis).
Definition: Let \(f\) be a function defined on some open interval that contains the number \(a\), except possibly at \(a\) itself. Then we say that the limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches \(a\) is \(L\), and we write \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\), if for every number \(\epsilon > 0\) there is a number \(\delta > 0\) such that:
\[ \text{if } 0 < |x - a| < \delta \text{ then } |f(x) - L| < \epsilon \]

title: Chapter 1: Limits and Continuity
text:
A function is continuous if you can draw its graph without lifting your pen. Mathematically:
A function \(f\) is continuous at a number \(a\) if: \[ \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a) \]
This implies three things: 1. \(f(a)\) is defined. 2. \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x)\) exists. 3. The limit equals the function value at that point.
